A solution of citric acid (equal to the total number of nitrate moles) was added to the nitrate solution. The heating source was then removed and the reaction mixture was allowed to cool down to the room temperature. Then, the reaction was brought to a pH 7 with ammonia solution. The temperature of the reaction mixture was raised to 80 °C and heated until the solution yielded a brownish gel. Afterward, it was followed by increasing the solution temperature to 300 °C. Due to spontaneous combustion, suddenly a flame was produced leading to the desired final product. The mixture was then calcined in a furnace at a temperature of 900 °C for 1 h in air.

Synthesis_Procedure: The ferric nitrate ninhydrate, strontium chloride dehydrate, and aluminium chlorite hexahydrate at a molar ratio of Sr2+: Al3+: Fe3+=1: 4: 8 were dissolved in the solution containing ethanol and water at ratio of 1:1 by stirring for 0.5 h. Then, sodium hydroxide aqueous solution was dropwisely slowly added into the solutions at room temperature with a constant stirring condition until pH = 9–10. After the coprecipitation was completed, the precipitate slurry was filtrated and washed with anhydrous ethanol until pH~7 and dried at 100°C for 10 h. Two portions of as-dried precursor were preheated at 300°C and 400°C for 1 h respectively. As-dried precursor and as-preheated precursors were heated at heating rate of 30°C/min, and then calcined at 900°C for 2 h and 3 h in air. The cooling was performed at a slow rate in furnace.

Synthesis_Procedure: M-type hexaferrite Sr0.65−xCaxLa0.35Fe11.32Co0.28O18.435 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.45) magnetic powder and magnets were prepared according to the Solid-state reaction method. The raw materials used in this paper were SrCO3 (97% purity), CaCO3 (99% purity), La2O3 (99% purity), Fe2O3 (98% purity), and Co2O3 (98% purity), mixed together in the stoichiometric composition of Sr0.65−xCaxLa0.35Fe11.32Co0.28O18.435 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.45). Mixtures of these raw materials were charged in a ball mill together with hardened steel balls with diameter of 8 mm. The powders were milled in water for 8 h with an angular velocity of 80 r/min and a ball-to-power weight ratio of 12:1. The as-milled powers were dried, crushed, and sifted. These samples were shaped into balls of about Φ 8 mm, and the temperature was increased up to 1260 °C in a box furnace; and these balls were calcined for 2 h in air. Then the calcined samples were dry-milled to particles under 100 μm using a vibration mill, then wet-milled with additives (CaCO3, SrCO3, SiO2, Cr2O3, Al2O3 or H3BO3) for 13 h using a ball-mill. The finely milled slurry with a diameter of about 0.75 μm was pressed into green pellets with Φ 30 × 15 mm by wet compacting under 310 MPa in a pulsed magnetic field of 900 kA/m, which was parallel to the pressing direction. The pressed pellets were sintered in a box furnace at 1210 °C–1200 °C for 1.5 h in air.

Synthesis_Procedure: M-type hexaferrites with formula SrFe12 − xAlxO19 (x =0.0, 1.5) were synthesized by means of the Pechini method. The following precursors were used: Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Mallinckrodt, ≥99.0%), Sr(NO)2 (Fluka ≥99.0%) and Al(NO)2·6H2O (Aldrich ≥98.0%). The synthetic route was the following: For each nitrate, weighed according to the stoichiometry of each composition, an individual dissolution in distilled water was prepared. After two hours of stirring, all the dissolutions were mixed in a single one. The polymeric resin was formed separately by the addition of citric acid and ethyleneglycol in the molar proportion 1:14, by heating at 70 °C during 30 min. At this point, the nitrates dissolution was added to the resin and kept under continuous stirring during 3 h at 90 °C, until the water evaporated. The resultant dried polymer was grounded for the following sequence of calcination treatments in a muffla (Thermolyne 47900): 200 °C for 12 h, 400 °C for 4 h, 700 °C for 18 h and 800 °C for 24 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The stoichiometric amounts of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Sr(NO3)2, Co(NO3)2·6H2O, ZrO(NO3)2, and Zn(NO3)2·6H2O were dissolved in distilled water and stirred until a homogeneous solution was obtained. Then, to this solution the citric acid as a chelating agent was added. The molar ratio of citric acid to metal cations was 1.2 : 1. The pH value of the solution was adjusted to 7 by using ammonia. The obtained solution was heated at 70°C under stirring to form a viscous gel, after which it was combusted by heating. Finally, the obtained powders were annealed at 900°C and the SrFe12O19 and SrFe11.1(ZrZn0.5Co0.5)0.45O19 powders were prepared. SrFe11.1(ZrZn0.5Co0.5)0.45O19 (0.75 g) and 2.7 mL aniline were added to 62 mL of 1 M hydrochloric acid solution, and it was then dispersed by ultrasonic for 40 min. Ammonium persulfate (6.67 g) was dissolved in 0.1 M hydrochloric acid solution, and the obtained solution was slowly added into the above mixture under stirring. The polymerization reaction was carried out at 0–4°C for 18 h. The mixture was filtered and washed with distilled water, 0.1 M HCl solution and ethanol to remove the remaining sulfate ions and aniline from it. Finally, the resultant was dried at 60°C for 24 h to obtain the polyaniline/SrFe11.1(ZrZn0.5Co0.5)0.45O19 composite.

Synthesis_Procedure: The chemicals used for the synthesis of different samples were Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Sigma-Aldrich, 98%), Sr(NO3)2 (Fluka, ≥99%), CoCl2·6H2O (Aldrich, 98%), ZrOCl2·4H2O (BDH, 96%), citric acid (Riedel-Dehaen, >99.5%) and ammonia solution (Riedel-Dehaen, 33%). They were used as such without any treatment. Strontium hexaferrites with nominal composition SrZrxCoxFe12 − 2xO19, where x =0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 were prepared by the sol–gel auto-combustion method keeping the molar ratio Fe/Sr=11.0. The molar ratio between citric acid and the metals was kept 1:1.5. Aqueous solutions of the required concentrations of all metal salts were mixed in a beaker on a hot plate with constant stirring. The aqueous solution of citric acid was also added in the beaker and the pH of the resultant solution was maintained at 7.0 by the addition of 2 M ammonia solution (all the solutions were prepared in the deionized water). Then the solution was evaporated slowly at 100 °C with constant stirring until it was converted into a viscous gel. Finally, the gel was burnt at 300 °C and the burnt brown powder was annealed at 950 °C for 5 h in a temperature programmed tube furnace (MTI GSL-1500X) to convert it into pure hexagonal phase. Eventually, the material was allowed natural cooling to room temperature.

Synthesis_Procedure: The SrFe12O19 powders were prepared using molten salt synthetic method. SrCO3, NaCl, KCl, K2SO4 and Na2SO4 were purchased from commercial sources (analytical grade) and used without any further purification. The oxidized scale used as ferrous material and the chemical composition is listed in Table 1. The reactants of oxidized scale and SrCO3 were weighted at a mole ratio of 5.3:1 (Fe2O3/SrCO3). The balls (10 mm), reactant and ethanol were load in zirconia vials (250 ml) and the ratio of these three weights was 10:1:1 and the ball-milling at a speed of 250 rpm for 10 h using Fritsch Pulverisette 4 planetary ball-mill. After evaporation of the ethanol at 80 °C for 10 h, the reactant was mixed with eutectic salts of NaCl–KCl, NaCl–Na2SO4, NaCl–K2SO4, KCl–K2SO4, KCl–Na2SO4, K2SO4–Na2SO4 with weight of 1:1, respectively. The powder mixtures were placed into an alumina crucible and heated to 1100 °C for 2 h. After that the crucibles were taken out from the muffle furnace cool to room temperature. The as-obtained powder was washed in hot distilled water; follow by filtration to remove the salts. After washing, the powders were dried at 80 °C for 12 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The sol–gel auto-combustion approach was utilized to synthesize the SrFe12O19. Analytical grade reagents were taken without extra purification. Glycine was used as fuel, and starting materials were Sr(NO3)3 and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O. The ratio of strontium and iron was taken as 1:12, and the proportion of metals and fuel was 1:13. According to material composition, the stoichiometric amount of metal nitrates was diffused in deionized water and they were individually stirred for 30 min. The ammonia solution was mixed with the solution to keep the pH level at 7. Then the aqueous solution was heated until it turned into gel form. The entire reaction got completed under constant magnetic stirring. As a result of heat supply, the self-combustion took place, and the gel got changed into particles. The burnt particles were ground nicely with the help of mortar and agate, and then the powder sintered at 1100 °C for 6 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The starting materials used for preparation of the samples were SrCO3 (Merck, 99 %), MnCO3 (Merck, 99.5%), TiO2 (Aldrich, 99.9%), NiO (Merck, 99%), and Fe2O3 (99.85%, from a domestic source). These materials mixed together in the composition of Sr:(Fe+ Mn+ Ni+ Ti)=1:(12) with a nominal formula of SrFe9 (Mn0.5 − xNixTi0.5)3O19 and x= 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5. The raw materials were thoroughly mixed and calcined at 1250 °C for 3 h in air. In order to get powders in the nanosized range, the crushed ferrites were milled again with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 8:1 by a SPEX mill for 1 h. Single phase unmilled and milled powders were cold pressed (3 tons/cm2) at room temperature into cylindrical shape with length, diameter and mass of about 7.4, 15.2 mm and 4.1 g, respectively. The cold-pressed nanosized samples were also annealed at different temperatures in air for 2 h and then free cooled to room temperature.

Synthesis_Procedure: A series of M-type strontium ferrite (SrFe12O19) crystal particles was prepared by hydrothermal synthesis using iron nitrate nonahydrate (AR 98.5%), strontium nitrate (AR 99.5%) and sodium hydroxide (AR 98.5%) as the starting materials. A quantity of mixed metal ions solution was added gradually to alkaline solution and the mixture was allowed to react at room temperature under magnetic stirring. Then, the composite slurry was transferred into a reaction kettle with agitating device and heat-treated at 220 °C for 2 hours. High purity nitrogen gas was charged into this closed system to regulate the initial pressure to 1.5 MPa. After the reaction was finished, the resultant precipitate was taken out from the kettle. Finally, the separated hexaferrite particles were washed several times with deionized water and absolute ethanol, dried at 80 °C and stored for subsequent use.

Synthesis_Procedure: The details of synthesis method of SrFe12−xCoxO19 (x = 0–1) nanoparticles by the sol-gel auto-combustion are as follows: first the inorganic precursors (Sr(NO3)2 , Fe(NO3)3 .9H2O, Co(NO3)2 .6H2O) in desired proportions corresponding to their stoichiometric formula (SrFe12−xCoxO19) were dissolved in deionized water by stirring on a hotplate at 50 °C. Then, citric acid was added to the above solution (citric acid to total metal ions molar ratio of 1:1), and subsequently stirred for 30 min at 70 °C. During continued heating at this temperature, the chelating between metal cations (Sr2+ , Fe3+ , Co2+ ) and citric acid as complexing agent is developed [27]. Afterward, the pH of the resulting mixture was adjusted at 7 by adding ammonia. Subsequently, the final solution was slowly heated for several hours at 80 °C with continuous stirring until it turned into high-viscosity wet gel. The obtained gel is then allowed to ignite in air through the auto-combustion reaction, and later was dried at 250 °C for 1 h. As a result of this reaction, an as-burnt product with a voluminous and treelike structure was obtained as shown in Fig. 1. In the final step of the sol-gel auto-combustion process, the as-burnt product was ground and then calcined at 1000 °C in air for 5 h with a heating rate of 5 °C/min to remove any organic residue and form the hexaferrite phase. The synthesis process of samples is also summarized in a flow chart shown in Fig. 2.

Synthesis_Procedure: Zn2+-Zr4+ substituted, barium-strontium hexaferrite (BaSrM) was synthesized using sol–gel auto combustion technique with a citric acid to metal nitrate ratio 1:1. Citric acid and nitrate salts of Barium, Strontium, Zinc, Zirconium and Fe3+ were dissolved in deionized water with constant magnetic stirring. The solution of ammonia was mixed drop wise using burette to bring pH of solution to 7. The resultant solution was heated at 80–100 °C for 6–8 h with continuous magnetic stirring. Dark brownish honey like gel was obtained with the evaporation of excessive water. Highly porous and fluffy precursor material was obtained after heating of gel at 200–250 °C for 1 h in the hot air oven. The precursor material was ground into fine powder form with mortar pastel. During calcination process (900 °C for 6 h at heating rate 100 °C/hr) the residual impurities were removed and half-cocked amorphous phase of BaSrM converted into crystalline phase. 2% PVA solution on the weight of BaSrM polycrystalline powder was mixed properly. Then properly dried, grinded and sieved powder was uniaxially pressed into 10 mm pellets at 7 metric tons pressure. These pellets were heated in alumina crucibles at 700 °C for 3 h to remove the PVA.

Synthesis_Procedure: All the starting reagents of analytical grade were used without further purification. The ferrites were prepared as per the following stoichiometric equation: Sr(CO3)2 + 12Fe(OH)3.xH2O —(ethylene glycol, fuel, oxidant, base; mixing, dehydration, ignition and combustion)→ SrFe12O19 Calculated amount of ferric nitrate was converted into ferric hydroxide by the addition of ammonia. The precipitates of ferric hydroxide were filtered and washed several times with distilled water and dissolved in hot citric acid/tartaric acid/sucrose/lactic acid solution (fuel:total metal 1.1:1). This was followed by addition of desired amounts of SrCO3 (Fe/Sr = 10.0, H2O2 was added to decompose SrCO3 and heated below 100 °C to expel out CO2 and excess H2O2) and ethylene glycol (10 % by volume of solution). The pH was settled at 7 by the addition of NH3 . NH4NO3 (NH4NO3 :total metal 1:1) was added as an oxidant. The reaction solution was stirred for 3 h and then heated slowly to obtain a highly viscous residue. The temperature was raised to 150 °C. The gel automatically ignited, burnt with glowing flints, and bubbled up with the evolution of gases. The material was finely ground and annealed at 600, 700, 800, 900, and 1000 °C for 6 h in a PID-controlled box furnace where the heating and cooling rates were maintained at 20 °C/min.

Synthesis_Procedure: In the present work, the samples weighing 10 g were prepared by mechanical alloying from the raw powders of Fe2O3 (99% purity) and SrCO3 (>97%), and they were mixed together in order to obtain a Sr/Fe ratio of 1 : 12. The milling processes were performed either in high-energy mill using 10 mm hardened steel balls, or in centrifugal planetary ball mill using three sizes of steel balls with diameters of 8, 10 or 12 mm. For the first sort of milling process using 10 mm balls in a high-energy mill, an angular velocity of 400 rpm and a ball to powder weight ratio of 7.5 : 1 were chosen. For other milling processes, a velocity of 125 rpm and two powder weight ratios of 15 : 1 and 7.5 : 1 were selected. Some as-milled samples were pressed at room temperature into rectangular specimens having a size of 4 × 1 × 0.5 cm 3. The calculated densities after pressing were about 4.0 g/cm 3, and similar to those of samples prepared by Ding et al. [8]. Both milling and pressing were performed in air. Most of the specimens obtained were annealed at different temperatures for a fixed time of 1 h. In addition, in order to study the detailed influence of annealing time on magnetic properties, one special kind of as-milled powder was chosen for heat treatment at 1000°C for a different time. Finally, the samples were rapidly quenched in air or cooled in the furnace for comparing the effect of the cooling condition on properties.

The milling processes were performed either in high-energy mill using 10 mm hardened steel balls, or in centrifugal planetary ball mill using three sizes of steel balls with diameters of 8, 10 or 12 mm. For the first sort of milling process using 10 mm balls in a high-energy mill, an angular velocity of 400 rpm and a ball to powder weight ratio of 7.5 : 1 were chosen. For other milling processes, a velocity of 125 rpm and two powder weight ratios of 15 : 1 and 7.5 : 1 were selected. Some as-milled samples were pressed at room temperature into rectangular specimens having a size of 4 × 1 × 0.5 cm 3. The calculated densities after pressing were about 4.0 g/cm 3, and similar to those of samples prepared by Ding et al. [8]. Both milling and pressing were performed in air. Most of the specimens obtained were annealed at different temperatures for a fixed time of 1 h. In addition, in order to study the detailed influence of annealing time on magnetic properties, one special kind of as-milled powder was chosen for heat treatment at 1000°C for a different time. Finally, the samples were rapidly quenched in air or cooled in the furnace for comparing the effect of the cooling condition on properties.

Synthesis_Procedure: The standard ceramic method is used to prepare M-type hexagonal ferrite samples with chemical formula Ba0.5Sr0.5CoxWxFe(12−2x)O19 (x = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0) [16]. AR grade of BaCo3 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany), SrCo3 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany), CoCO3 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany), WO2 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany) and Fe2O3 (99.99% purity, E-Merck, Germany) were used as starting materials. The stoichiometric amount of different chemical reagents of compositions was grounded in an agate pestle and mortar in the distilled water for 8 h. The ground mixed powders were pre-sintered at 1000 °C for 10 h in microcontroller programmed an electric furnace and recovered powders were reground under the same conditions in order to produce fine powder material. The sieving of powders was carried out with sieves of mesh size 220 B.S.S. After adding polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) in fine powder; pellets of each composition were prepared, using a hydraulic press under a uniaxial pressure of 75 kN/m2. The final sintering of pellets was carried out at 1150 °C for 15 h. The heating and cooling rates of an electric furnace were set to ±5 °C.

Synthesis_Procedure: The Ba0.5Sr0.5-xGdxFe12.0-xZnxO19 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.4) hexaferrites were synthesized by sol-gel auto-combustion method. All the precursors were of analytical grade, weighed according to the stoichiometric calculations. A stoichiometric mixture solution was prepared by dissolving Ba(NO3)2, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Gd(NO3)3·6H2O, Zn(NO3)3·6H2O and C6H8O7 acid in deionized water. The mole ratio of total metal ions to citric acid was 1:1. NH4OH solution was then added to keep the pH value of the solution at 7. The solution was evaporated gently at 80 °C under a constant stirring until the solution appeared to be more viscous with the final form of a brownish gel. As the temperature was steadily increasing up to 150 °C and the gel started burning out. After this, the powders were grinded in an agate mortar and pestle. In order to achieve M-type hexaferrite phase, the crushed powders were annealed in a muffle furnace at temperature of 1200 °C for 2 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The chemicals used in the synthesis of strontium hexaferrite and its Bi–Cr substituted derivatives were Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Riedel-dehaem, 97%), Bi(NO3)3·5H2O (Sigma, 98%), Sr(NO3)2 (Harris chemical, 99.99%), Cr(NO3)3·9H2O (Merck, 99.99%), HNO3 (Merck, 65%), ethylene glycol (Fluka, 99%) and NH3 (Merck, 35%). These chemicals were used as such without further treatment. The strontium hexaferrite with nominal composition SrFe12 − xBixCrxO19 (where x =0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1) was prepared by the sol–gel method. The solutions of required molarities for the required metal salts were prepared by dissolving the stoichiometric amounts in deionized water. Bismuth nitrate is insoluble in water and was dissolved in minimum volume of nitric acid and then diluted to required volume with deionized water. The solutions were mixed in a 500 mL beaker and stirred using magnetic stirrer with controlled thermostat. The stoichiometric amount of ethylene glycol was added as a chelating agent. The solution mixture was heated up to 60 °C with continuous stirring on a hot plate. The 2.0 M ammonium hydroxide was added drop wise to adjust pH to 7 and then the solution was evaporated slowly by heating at 80 °C with continuous stirring. The sol is transformed into a brown gel after the water evaporation. The gel was then burned by heating at 300 °C to obtain the powder which was finally annealed at 950 °C for 5 h in an electric furnace (VULCAN™ A550).

Synthesis_Procedure: To prepare MFe12O19 (M = Ba, Pb, Sr) hexaferrites, Ba(NO3)2⋅4H2O, Pb(NO3)2⋅4H2O, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, ammonia (NH3), and citric acid (C6H8O7.H2O) as raw materials were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and used without further purification. For the synthesis of single-phase hexaferrites by the citrate-nitrate method, firstly, we investigated the effect of the synthesis parameters, such as the iron-to-barium molar ratio (10, 11, and 12), the nitrate-tocitrate ratio (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2, 4, and 6), and the heating temperature (750, 850, and 950 °C) at pH 7 for the formation reaction of pure-phase BaFe12O19. The results (not included here) showed that pure-phase BaFe12O19 powders can be obtained through the citrate-nitrate process with an iron-to-barium molar ratio of 11, a nitrate-to-citrate ratio of 1.5, and a heating temperature of 850 °C at pH 7. However, the pH has too much of an effect on the morphology, decreasing the optimum calcination temperature and the formation of single-phase hexaferrites. The literature shows that the pH can be considered as the key factor for controlling the ferrite nanostructure, and optimal physical properties are found at pH 7 [35,36]. Therefore, to prepare MFe12O19 (M = Ba, Pb, Sr) hexaferrites, specified amounts of the raw materials, Ba(NO3)2⋅4H2O, Pb (NO3)2⋅4H2O, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and citric acid, were completely dissolved in the minimum amount of deionized water (solution) with a nitrate-to-citrate molar ratio of 1.5:1. Then ammonia (NH3) was added to adjust the pH to 7 under stirring. The resulting solution was heated in an oil bath kept at 200 °C for 24 h to evaporate water. The resulting wet gels of high viscosity were then placed in an oven at 200 °C for 2 h to form a dry gel. The powders obtained were put in a furnace at 850 °C for 4 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: All chemicals (acquired from Sigma-Aldrich and Vetec) used to synthesize SrFe12-xSmxO19 (0≤x≤0.15) powders were of high purity (> 99.9%) and were used without further purification. During a typical synthesis, Sr(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3.9H2O were weighed stoichiometrically and then completely dissolved in filtered (Unifil 80 g/cm2) coconut water (Cocos mucifera), [38]. In the synthesis, Fe3+ : Sr2+ molar ratio was fixed at 12:1. The system remained under agitation until it achieved complete homogenization. Upon completion, the initial solution had its pH adjusted to 5.0 through the addition of ammonium hydroxide at 30%. We maintained the agitation until the formation of the sol. Afterwards, we heated the sol up to 100 °C and kept on constant temperature for 24 h to dehydrate. The result was a very porous and low-density solid material (xerogel). This material was heated at 500 °C for 2 hours (with a heating and cooling rate of 2 °C/min) to decompose the initial salts and remove the organic phase. After cooling, the material was homogenized and calcined at 1000 °C for 2h in open atmosphere with a heating and cooling rate of 2 °C/min. The production of the doped material followed the same procedure, but the strontium salt Sr(NO3)2 was mixed to the samarium salt (Sm(NO3)3.6H2O) in the following ratios: 5%; 10% and 15%.

Synthesis_Procedure: All chemicals (acquired from Sigma-Aldrich and Vetec) used to synthesize SrFe12-xSmxO19 (0≤x≤0.15) powders were of high purity (> 99.9%) and were used without further purification. During a typical synthesis, Sr(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3.9H2O were weighed stoichiometrically and then completely dissolved in filtered (Unifil 80 g/cm2) coconut water (Cocos mucifera), [38]. In the synthesis, Fe3+ : Sr2+ molar ratio was fixed at 12:1. The system remained under agitation until it achieved complete homogenization. Upon completion, the initial solution had its pH adjusted to 5.0 through the addition of ammonium hydroxide at 30%. We maintained the agitation until the formation of the sol. Afterwards, we heated the sol up to 100 °C and kept on constant temperature for 24 h to dehydrate. The result was a very porous and low-density solid material (xerogel). This material was heated at 500 °C for 2 hours (with a heating and cooling rate of 2 °C/min) to decompose the initial salts and remove the organic phase. After cooling, the material was homogenized and calcined at 1000 °C for 2h in open atmosphere with a heating and cooling rate of 2 °C/min. The production of the doped material followed the same procedure, but the strontium salt Sr(NO3)2 was mixed to the samarium salt (Sm(NO3)3.6H2O) in the following ratios: 5%; 10% and 15%.

Synthesis_Procedure: The chemical precursors used for these experiments are Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Sr(NO3)2 , Pr(NO3)3·6H2O and NaOH. The precursors were weighted according to different Pr3+ /Sr2+ ratios (n = Pr3+ /Sr3+ ), where n was varied between 1/16 and 1/4, while Sr2+ /Fe3+ and [NO3 − ]/[OH− ] ratios were fixed at 1/8 and 1/2, respectively. A water solution containing Sr2+ , Fe3+ and Pr3+ ions was poured into the solution of NaOH. Aqueous suspensions containing the precipitated products were stirred at 1000 rpm and heated to 220 °C for 3 h in an autoclave at a pressure of 25 bar [13]. The resultant particles were carefully washed and filtered using deionised water, and then dried overnight at 80 °C. In order to homogenise the materials and improve the magnetic properties, the as-synthesised particles were then calcined at temperatures from 1000 to 1250 °C for 2 h in air.

Synthesis_Procedure: The standard ceramic method is used to prepare M-type hexagonal ferrite samples with compositions Ba0.5Sr0.5CoxAlxFe(12−2x)O19 (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0) [13]. AR grade of BaCo3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98% pure), SrCo3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98%), CoCO3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98% pure), Al2O3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98% pure), Fe2O3 (Sigma-Aldrich 99.98% pure) used as starting materials. The stoichiometric amount of different chemical reagents of compositions was grounded in an agate pestle and mortar in the distilled water for 8 h and ground mixed powders were then presintered at 1000 °C for 10 h in an electric furnace and obtained powders were reground under the same conditions in order to produce fine material. The sieving of powders was carried out with sieves of mesh size 220 B.S.S. and powders were pressed into pellets using a hydraulic press under an uniaxial pressure of 75 kN/m2 and the final sintering of pellets was carried out at 1250 °C for 20 h, followed by furnace cooling to room temperature in order to increase the density of prepared material and to obtain desired product of Ba0.5Sr0.5CoxAlxFe(12−2x)O19 (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0) hexagonal ferrite powders. The heating and cooling rates were set to ±5 °C.

Synthesis_Procedure: The chemicals used for the preparation of the samples were Ba(NO3)2 (99%, Sigma Aldrich), Sr(NO3)2·4H2O (98%, Sigma Aldrich), and FeCl3·9H2O (97%, Sigma Aldrich), Al(NO3)3 4H2O (98%, Sigma Aldrich) and Tb2O3 (99%, Sigma Aldrich). The stock solution of each chemical in de-ionized water was prepared in a 100 ml beaker by using stoichiometric amounts of the respective metal salts and stirred for 15 min. The solutions of the required concentrations were mixed in a 1000 ml Pyrex beaker and heated at a constant temperature of 80 °C under constant stirring on a hot plate with magnetic stirrer. The citric acid was added to the metal solution and kept the molar ratio between metal and citric acid 1:1.5. Ammonia solution was added to adjust the pH value to 7.0. The solution was slowly evaporated at 80 °C until a viscous gel is formed. The temperature of the hot plate magnetic stirrer was increased up to about 200 °C for the ignition of the gel. The dried gel burnt in a self-propagating combustion manner until all of it was completely burnt out as brown colored fluffy powders. The gel was heated at 500 °C for 4 h to decompose the organic precursor in the digitally controlled microwave oven ‘‘Wise Ven Fuzy Control System’’. The powders were pressed into pellets of size (3.5 mm thickness and 8 mm diameter) under a force of 30 kN by using the Paul Otto Webber hydraulic press. The sintering of the powders and pellets was carried out simultaneously at 1100 °C for 5 h in a furnace ‘‘Hobersal model HD-230’’ to convert it into hexagonal phase. The synthesis steps are shown in Fig. 1.

Synthesis_Procedure: The glass of the initial composition SrFe8Cr4O19 –12Sr2B2O5 was prepared by rapid melt quenching. For that purpose, the stochiometric mixture of the starting reagents (SrCO3, Fe2O3, H3BO3, and Cr2O3, high purity grade, Aldrich, Saint Louis, MO, USA) was homogenized into a 10 g batch and fired at 900 °C for 2 h; then, the batch was ground and melted in a platinum crucible at 1350 °C. After a 1 h exposure, the melt was quenched between two rotating steel rollers to form glassy flakes. Synthesis_Procedure: In this experiment, Sr1-xTbxFe12-yCoyO19 (x = 0.04 mol; y = 0.0, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50 mol) ferrite was prepared by ceramic sintering. Raw materials required for the experiment: iron oxide powder (Mackin, 99%), strontium carbonate powder (Mackin, 99.9%), terbium pentoxide powder (Chinese rare earths, 99.99%), cobalt oxide powder (Mackin, 99.9%), the raw materials to be weighed are calculated according to the proportion of molar percentage. The raw material is put into the ball mill for ball grinding, the speed is set at 550 r/min, and the ball grinding time is 4 h. The mixture after ball milling is poured into the beaker to settle, and the sediment is put into the drying box for drying. The temperature of the drying box is set at 150 °C and the drying time is 5 h. The dried mixture was ground and sieved, and the ground powder was put into the Muffle furnace for high temperature pre-burning, the processing temperature was 1180 °C, the pre-burning time was set to 3 h, and finally the strontium ferrite powder sample was obtained. The powder sample is put into the ball mill for secondary ball milling. The purpose of secondary ball milling is to make the strontium ferrite powder more uniform, which is convenient for subsequent compaction treatment. The strontium ferrite powder was divided into two parts, and one part was used to test the properties of the powder. Another strontium ferrite powder was pressed. The pressed block ferrite was put into the Muffle furnace for high temperature sintering, the sintering temperature was set at 1200 °C, and the sintering time was 3 h. Finally, the block M-type strontium ferrite was obtained, and the block ferrite was polished and polished on the surface to reduce the error of the subsequent magnetic properties test. The preparation process is shown in Fig. 2.

Synthesis_Procedure: Sb-doped strontium hexaferrite powders, SrFe12-xSbxO19 (x = 0.00, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08), were synthesized via a sol-gel auto-combustion route. Analytical grade precursors viz., strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2], ferric nitrate nano-hydrate [Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O] citric acid monohydrate and ethylene glycol were used. Stoichiometric amounts of Sr(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O were dissolved separately in 30 mL and 50 mL of deionized water respectively. The resulting solutions were then mixed under continuous stirring. Citric acid monohydrate was then introduced into the solution maintaining the metal ion to citric acid ratio at 1:1.5 to ensure effective chelation and prevent undesirable precipitation of metal ions. The mixed solution was maintained at 80 °C under continuous stirring at 400 rpm in a magnetic hot plate for 2 h. For Sb doping, the appropriate amount of Sb2O3 was dispersed in 1.5 mL of concentrated nitric acid and 2 mL of deionized water, followed by heating for 20 min and ultrasonication for 30 min to ensure dissolution. The cooled Sb solution was added dropwise to the metal–citric acid solution under constant magnetic stirring. Ethylene glycol was then added in a 1:1 M ratio with citric acid to facilitate gel formation and promote thorough mixing. As the gel became increasingly viscous, the stirrer was removed. The temperature was gradually increased to ~150 °C, and the gel was then transferred to a heating mantle for uniform heating and to initiate auto-combustion, yielding a voluminous and porous precursor powder. The resulting ash residue was ground and calcined at 900 °C for 4 h to obtain phase purity. The calcined powder obtained was then mixed with 2 wt% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as a binder and thoroughly ground to ensure uniform mixing. The powder was then uniaxially pressed into circular pellets of 8 mm diameter under an applied pressure of approximately 100 kg/cm2 using a hydraulic press. The pellets were sintered at 1100 °C for 3 h to achieve sufficient densification and enhance mechanical strength.

Stoichiometric amounts of Sr(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O were dissolved separately in 30 mL and 50 mL of deionized water respectively. The resulting solutions were then mixed under continuous stirring. Citric acid monohydrate was then introduced into the solution maintaining the metal ion to citric acid ratio at 1:1.5 to ensure effective chelation and prevent undesirable precipitation of metal ions. The mixed solution was maintained at 80 °C under continuous stirring at 400 rpm in a magnetic hot plate for 2 h. For Sb doping, the appropriate amount of Sb2O3 was dispersed in 1.5 mL of concentrated nitric acid and 2 mL of deionized water, followed by heating for 20 min and ultrasonication for 30 min to ensure dissolution. The cooled Sb solution was added dropwise to the metal–citric acid solution under constant magnetic stirring. Ethylene glycol was then added in a 1:1 M ratio with citric acid to facilitate gel formation and promote thorough mixing. As the gel became increasingly viscous, the stirrer was removed. The temperature was gradually increased to ~150 °C, and the gel was then transferred to a heating mantle for uniform heating and to initiate auto-combustion, yielding a voluminous and porous precursor powder. The resulting ash residue was ground and calcined at 900 °C for 4 h to obtain phase purity. The calcined powder obtained was then mixed with 2 wt% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as a binder and thoroughly ground to ensure uniform mixing. The powder was then uniaxially pressed into circular pellets of 8 mm diameter under an applied pressure of approximately 100 kg/cm2 using a hydraulic press. The pellets were sintered at 1100 °C for 3 h to achieve sufficient densification and enhance mechanical strength.

Synthesis_Procedure: The pure phase hexagonal ferrite, BaFe12-xSmxO19 with (x = 0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0) is prepared using a low cost citrate precursor sol–gel method. Chemicals used in this synthesis process were of high purity grade namely, Ba (NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3 and Sm (NO3)2 (Alfa Aesar, 99.9% purity). Citric acid worked as fuel during synthesis. The stoichiometric ratio of citric acid to metal cations was maintained to be 1:3 during solution preparation. At first, we weigh calculated proportion of chemical nitrates and dissolve it into individual beakers containing minimal amount of deionized water. Followed by pouring of these individual solutions into a single beaker and shifting the pH of this solution to 7 using drop wise addition of ammonia. Then this solution is kept on hot plate magnetic stirrer at temperature of 120℃ under continuous stirring, till a viscous like material is visible. In next step, this viscous jelly like substance is transferred into a hot air oven set at temperature 250℃ for 1 h for self-propagating combustion reaction to occur. As such we get a fluffy like ash powder, which is crushed down to fine powders using mortar and pestle. The powdered samples were then put into a microprocessor based annealing furnace, in alumina crucibles separately at 850℃ for 2 h each, with a heating rate of 4℃/ min.

Synthesis_Procedure: The M-type SrCaLa hexaferrites with chemical compositions of Sr0.5Ca0.2La0.3Fe12.0−2x(SnMg)xO19 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5) were synthesized by ball milling and calcining. The starting materials used in this study were SrCO3 (99% purity), CaCO3 (99% purity), La2O3 (99% purity), Fe2O3 (99% purity), SnO2 (99% purity) and MgO (99% purity). They were used as such without further treatment. The starting powders were weighted in accordance with the ratios of the chemical composition. A ball mill was used with a ball to powder of 10:1. The milling was carried out for 9 h with a rotate speed of 80 rpm. After milling, the mixed powders were dried in a drying oven in the air, and then calcined in a muffle furnace at 1250 °C for 2.0 h in air. Next, the calcined samples were shattered to particles less than 50 lm by a vibration mill. In order to relieve the stress, the shattered particles were annealed in a muffle furnace at 780 °C for 1.5 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: BaM doped with Zn2+-Zr4+ was synthesized via sol-gel auto combustion methods using metal nitrate to fuel (citric acid) ratio of 1:1.5. Analytical grade chemicals such as ferric nitrate, Barium nitrate, zinc nitrate, zirconyl nitrate and citric acid were used without further purification. Metal salts were dissolved in double distilled water in stoichiometric ratio separately and then citric acid was added at ambient temperature with constant magnetic stirring. Ammonia was added drop wise to adjusted pH 7. The resultant solution was heated at 80-100°C for 3-4 hours with continuous magnetic stirring. With continuous heating excessive water evaporates and honey like highly viscous brown gel was formed. This gel was put in oven at 200-250°C for 1-2 hour after which auto combustion occurs resulting in a precursor powder material. The precursor material was grounded with motor pastel into fine powder form. Further this powder was calcined at 900°C for 6 hours in muffle furnace to remove impurities and half-baked M-Type BAM amorphous phase into single domain crystalline phase.

Analytical grade chemicals such as ferric nitrate, Barium nitrate, zinc nitrate, zirconyl nitrate and citric acid were used without further purification. Metal salts were dissolved in double distilled water in stoichiometric ratio separately and then citric acid was added at ambient temperature with constant magnetic stirring. Ammonia was added drop wise to adjusted pH 7. The resultant solution was heated at 80-100°C for 3-4 hours with continuous magnetic stirring. With continuous heating excessive water evaporates and honey like highly viscous brown gel was formed. This gel was put in oven at 200-250°C for 1-2 hour after which auto combustion occurs resulting in a precursor powder material. The precursor material was grounded with motor pastel into fine powder form. Further this powder was calcined at 900°C for 6 hours in muffle furnace to remove impurities and half-baked M-Type BAM amorphous phase into single domain crystalline phase.

Synthesis_Procedure: Desired metal nitrates in appropriate ratios were taken in the minimum amount of distilled water followed by the addition of citric acid (citric acid to total metal ions =1:1) and stirred until a homogenous mixture was obtained. The molar ratio of strontium was kept higher, i.e. 1.2, to maintain the stoichiometry of the product in these samples because of higher solubility of Sr(NO3)2 as compared to Fe(NO3)3.9H2O. The total weight of starting materials was 20 g. The pH was settled at 7 by the addition of NH4OH (35%) solution drop by drop using vigorous stirring at 70 °C. Dehydration of the solution was then carried out on a hotplate at 80 °C until a brown gel was formed. Dry gels prepared were heated in air at 220 °C to invoke ignition. Upon ignition,a large amount of gases were liberated and a light weight voluminous powder was formed quickly (Fig. 1). The material was finely ground and calcinated at 1100 °C for 5 h in a muffle furnace where the heating rates were maintained at 5 °C/min. The material was allowed to naturally cool and compressed at 8 t to make pellets of 10 mm diameter and of 2 mm thickness.

Synthesis_Procedure: The hexaferrite samples of stoichiometric formula Sr0.54Ca0.46AlxFe12-xO19 (SCAFO - x) with Al doping concentration x = 2.0, 4.0, 5.5 and 6.5 were prepared by a standard solid-state reaction method which involves the reaction of Strontium Carbonate (SrCO3), Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3), Iron oxide (Fe2O3) and Aluminum oxide (Al2O3) in appropriate molecular ratios according to the reaction as follows: 54SrCO3 + 46CaCO3 + (1-x)Fe2O3 + xAl2O3 → Sr0.54Ca0.46AlxFe12-xO19 + CO2 (1) A schematic representation of the hexaferrite synthesis process is shown in Fig. 1(a). High purity powders of SrCO3, CaCO3, Fe2O3, and Al2O3 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.9% purity) were weighed according to their stoichiometric ratios, thoroughly mixed and ground for 12 h in an agate mortar using isopropyl alcohol as a wet grinding medium to ensure a homogeneous compound mixture. The resulting powder, corresponding to different hexaferrite compositions, was then calcined at an optimized temperature of 1350 °C for 24 h (Fig. 1(b)). To achieve uniformity, the calcined powders were reground in a mortar and pestle for 2–3 h with a small amount of binder (3% polyvinyl alcohol aqueous solution). The obtained powders were subsequently pressed uniaxially under a pressure of 3000 psi using a stainless-steel die punch, forming pellets with approximate dimensions of 10 mm in diameter and 3 mm in thickness. These pellets were then sintered at a temperature of 1400 °C for 6 h, following a controlled heating and cooling rate of 5 °C/min in a programmable muffle furnace.

Synthesis_Procedure: Strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2, ACS reagent, 99.0% purity), iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, ACS reagent, 98.0% purity), aluminium nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO3)3.9H2O, ACS reagent, 98.0% purity), calcium nitrate (Ca(NO3)2, ACS reagent, 97.0% purity), Manganese nitrate tetrahydrate (Mn(NO3)2.4H2O, ACS reagent, 98.0% purity) as inorganic reactants were used as the initial salt for the synthesis of pure and cation substituted SFO. All the chemicals were purchased from Alfa Aesar. Citric acid (C6H8O7) was used as chelating agent, Ammonium Hydroxide (NH4OH) (Make: Merck) was used as pH adjuster, and deionized water as the solvent. The starting precursors were all of analytical purity and used without further purification. Sr0.8Ca0.2Fe10Al2-yMnyO19 (0 ≤ y ≤ 2) has been synthesized using the SGAC method with Fe/Sr molar ratio of 9.23:1, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 2. The inorganic salts (Sr(NO3)2, (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O), (Al (NO3)3.9H2O), Ca(NO3)2, and Mn(NO3)2.4H2O were dissolved in deionized water and stirred on a hotplate at 70 °C. After a clear solution was obtained, C6H8O7 was added to the above solution (citric acid to total metal ions molar ratio of 1:1), and subsequently stirred on hot plate at 90 °C. Afterward, the pH of the resulting mixture was adjusted to 7 by dropwise addition of NH4OH using a pipette. Subsequently, the final solution was continuously stirred for several hours at 90 °C until a highly viscous wet gel was formed. The obtained gel was then allowed to ignite in air through the auto-combustion reaction. As a result of this reaction, an as-burnt product with a voluminous and treelike structure was obtained. Then the obtained products were collected and crushed using an agate mortar pastel. The as-prepared powders were calcined in a muffle furnace at 950 °C for 1 h at a heating rate of 10 °C/min in air ambient.

Synthesis_Procedure: This study reports the fabrication of hexagonal ferrite ceramics with the nominal composition BaFe11.5CuxZn0.25-xSn0.25O19 (x = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20) via a conventional solid-state reaction sintering route. Highpurity BaCO3 (99.0%, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., lot No. 20250530), Fe2O3 (99%, reagent grade, Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd., lot No. C17524742), CuO (≥99.0%, analytical grade, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., lot No. 20250312), ZnO (≥99.0%, pharmaceutical test grade, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., lot No. 20250113), and SnO2 (≥99.95%, metals basis, Aladdin Industrial Corporation, lot No. E2528656) powders were weighed according to the stoichiometric ratios and subjected to planetary ball milling at 250 rpm for 12 h in ethanol to ensure homogeneous mixing. Synthesis_Procedure: We synthesized polycrystalline BaFe8Al2Zn2O19 hexaferrite using a sol-gel auto-combustion method. We dissolved analytical-grade barium, iron, aluminum, and zinc nitrates in deionized water according to the stoichiometry of the above-mentioned composition. Citric acid was added as a chelating agent and fuel for combustion. The pH of the solution was carefully maintained at approximately 7 by slowly adding aqueous ammonia [33]. The mixture was heated to approximately 85 °C while being stirred with a magnet until it formed a thick gel. Subsequently, heat treatment caused self-ignition at approximately 250 °C, resulting in a fine, ash-like powder. First, the burned powder was carefully ground to ensure that the particles were evenly spread out. Then, it was pre-calcined in air at 900 °C for 4 h to remove any organic material and initiate the crystallization process. Subsequently, the powder was pressed into pellets (≈5 mm radius, ≈2 mm thickness) at a pressure of 300 MPa. Sintering in ambient air was performed at 1200, 1225, 1250, 1275, and 1300 °C for 4 h. The sintering temperature range of 1200–1300 °C was selected based on prior literature on Al/Znsubstituted BaM hexaferrites, which indicates phase formation and optimal densification occur within this window, and was further supported by preliminary experiments assessing phase purity and microstructural evolution. The temperature was increased and decreased at a rate of 5 °C/min to prevent the grains from growing too large [34]. Fig. 1 shows a schematic overview of the entire synthesis process.

Synthesis_Procedure: The entire explored poly-crystalline sintered Sr1-xCexFe12-xCoxO19 (0≤x≤0.25/x=0.05) nano hexaferrites (SCFCO-N-Hs) were synthesized by mixing of highly graded pure Fe2O3 (98%), SrCO3 (99%), Ce2O3 (99%), and CoO (99%) powders under the conventional solid-state reaction approach. Figure 1 shows the synthesization steps of the process. Primarily, the entire preparatory materials were heterogeneous in an indented stoichiometric ratio of 1:12. Then the blend of these rare compounds was refined in distilled water and milled at an angular frequency of 300 rpm for 2 hours in a planetary ball milling mechanism (Pulverisette; Fritsch GmbH, Germany), with hardened steel balls of diameter 8 mm, 10 mm, and 12 mm. The ball to powder ratio elected as 10:1 and the ball-to-ball ratio was 1:1.5:2. The extracted wet powder mixture then filtered, dried, and crushed. The execration of SCFCO-N-Hs powders is as follows, (1-x)SrCO3 + ((12−x)/2)Fe2O3 + xCoO + (x/2)Ce2O3 → SrxCexFe12−xCoxO19 + CO2 ↑ These dried powder samples then sintered in a box coke oven for 2 hours at 1260 C0. After that, the calcite samples milled into powder of particles sizes less than 100 nm in a vibrating mill.

Synthesis_Procedure: The SrFe10−xNixAl2O19 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.3) hexaferrite powders were prepared by using sol–gel auto-combustion method. High-purity chemicals including strontium nitrate Sr(NO3)2·4H2O (Sigma–Aldrich, ≥99%), iron nitrate Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (Sigma– Aldrich, ≥98%), nickel nitrate Ni(NO3)2·6H2O (LobaChemie, ≥98%), and aluminum nitrate Al(NO3)3·9H2O (Sigma–Aldrich, ≥98%) were individually dissolved in distilled water. Then the solutions were combined in a single beaker and stirred magnetically until obtaining a homogeneous solution. Citric acid (Sigma–Aldrich, ≥ 99.5%) was added in a 1:2 ratio to the solution, followed by neutralization with ammonia. After approximately 3 h of stirring at 80 °C on a hot plate, a viscous liquid gel was formed. Synthesis_Procedure: The sol-gel auto-combustion method was adopted as the synthesis technique for the present work. Strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2], ferric nitrate [Fe(NO3)3·9H2O], aluminum nitrate [Al(NO3)3·9H2O], nickel nitrate [Ni(NO3)2.6H2O], cobalt nitrate [Co(NO3)2·6H2O], and glycine (C2H5NO2) of AR grade were used and metal nitrate versus fuel ratio was taken as 1:1. The number of moles taken for each compound is represented through the reaction given below (where x = 0.1, 0.2): [1 − x]Sr(NO3)2 + [10]Fe(NO3)3·9H2O + [2]Al(NO3)3·9H2O + [x][Ni(NO3)2·6H2O/Co(NO3)2·6H2O] + C2H5NO2 + NH4OH → [Sr1−xNixAl2Fe10O19/Sr1−xCoxAl2Fe10O19] + NH3 ↑ + CO2 ↑ + NOχ ↑ + H2O ↑ (1) The stoichiometry amount of each metal nitrate was dissolved in the di-ionized water and stirred for 30 min. Later, all the metal nitrate solutions were mixed, and the glycine solution was added to it; then the solution was given heat, and it was kept at 80 °C for 30 min. To neutralize the solution (pH = 7), the ammonia solution (NH4OH) was added to it. Then continuous heat was provided to the solution until it changed into a gel form, and the constant supply of heat resulted in a self-auto-combustion reaction. Then the burnt powder was ground using agate and mortar and was sintered at 1100 °C for 4 h. Afterwards, the final compound was used for various characterizations (Fig. 1). For the dielectric studies, pellets of diameter of 1 cm and thickness of 2 mm were prepared.

We weighed six groups of drugs according to different molar ratios, put the weighed samples into a nylon tank, and mixed the balls, materials, and water at a ratio of 10:1:1.1. The homogenized slurry was dried and pressed into a muffle furnace for sintering at a heating rate of 5 °C/min up to 1240 °C, held for 2 h, and then cooled via furnace cooling. Synthesis_Procedure: Ba0.54Ca0.46Fe12− x AlxO19 (x = 2.3, 2.4 and 2.5) powders were synthesized via sol-gel auto-combustion method. Aluminium nitrate Al (NO3)3.6H2O (Sigma Aldrich, ≥98%), Iron nitrates Fe(NO3)3.9H2O (Sigma Aldrich, ≥98%), Calcium nitrates Ca(NO3)2.4H2O (Sigma Aldrich, ≥99%) and Barium nitrates Ba(NO3)2 (Sigma Aldrich, ≥99%), were dissolved separately in distilled water, then the solutions of Iron, aluminium, calcium and barium nitrates were mixed in a larger beaker under continuous stirring. Subsequently, an aqueous solution of citric acid C6H8O7 was introduced into the metal-nitrate solution, maintaining a molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid of 1:1, then a solution of Ammonia hydroxide was added to the solution to maintain the pH at 7. The solution was heated at 80 °C until obtaining a gel, the gel was after that heated at 200 °C until it is spontaneously burned and turned into a voluminous porous powder. The obtained gel was crushed and annealed in air at 1250 °C for 3 h, with a heating rate of 3 °C per minute.

Synthesis_Procedure: The Ba0.5Sr0.5DyxFe12-xO19 (0.00 ≤ x ≤ 0.15) samples were prepared via the sol-gel auto-combustion technique, which is well-suited for obtaining homogeneous and fine-grained hexaferrite powders. The Analytical-grade Ba(NO3)2, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and Dy (NO3)3⋅xH2O (≥99.9% purity, Sigma-Aldrich) were used as precursor salts without further purification. In a typical synthesis procedure, stoichiometric amount of Barium nitrate [Ba(NO3)2], Strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2], Ferric nitrate nonahydrate [Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O], and Dysprosium nitrate [Dy(NO3)3⋅xH2O] were accurately weighed and dissolved in DI water under continuous magnetic stirring to form a clear and uniform aqueous solution. Citric acid was employed as a chelating and fuel agent and it was added to the solution in a molar ratio of 3:1 relative to the total metal cations for the combustion process. The resulting mixture was then gently heated to approximately 80 °C with constant stirring until it transformed into a viscous gel, indicating successful complexation between the metal ions and citric acid. To facilitate proper gelation and maintain a near-neutral pH, ammonia solution was introduced gradually in a dropwise manner until the pH reached around 7. Once the gel was formed, it was subjected to further heating, leading to spontaneous ignition and combustion. This exothermic reaction produced a voluminous, fluffy precursor powder. The precursor was finely milled with an agate mortar and pestle to achieve homogeneous particle size prior to calcination. Calcination was performed in a muffle furnace at 1100 °C for 5 h, resulting in phase-pure hexaferrite powders ready for further structural and magnetic analyses.

Synthesis_Procedure: The BaFe12-xMnxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4) powders were prepared by hydrothermal synthesis. The precursor was a mixture of an aqueous solution of iron nitrate nonahydrate Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, barium nitrate Ba(NO3)2 and manganese chloride MnCl2⋅4H2O with an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide NaOH in proportion 60 ml/20 ml, respectively. The solutions were prepared with the expectation that in the final volume (80 mL) the concentration of iron ions would be 0.25 M, the (Fe3++Mn2+)/Ba2+ ratio would be 9, and the OH/NO3 ratio would be 2.5. After that, the resulting mixture was placed in a 100 ml Teflon vessel, hermetically sealed and placed in an oven. The autoclave was slowly heated to 180 oC over 2 h and maintained at this temperature for 4 h. The resulting precipitate and liquid solution were separated using a centrifuge. The precipitate was washed and dried at 90 °C for 8 h. The dry residue was ground in an agate mortar and annealed in a muffle furnace in air. The heating rate was 15° /min, the final temperature was 900 °C, and the annealing time was 1 h. To remove possible side phases, the samples were washed in hydrochloric acid HCl (10%) and distilled water and then sent back to the drying oven for 8 h at a temperature of 90 °C.

Synthesis_Procedure: Rare earth-substituted strontium hexaferrite samples (Sr1-xRExFe12O19) were synthesized using the Pechini sol-gel method, targeting substitution levels of x = 0.01, 0.025, 0.050, 0.075, and 0.10. Additionally, unsubstituted strontium hexaferrite (x = 0.0) was prepared to use as a reference. The synthesis was carried out using chemical reagents and solvents such as strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2, Meyer, 99%), iron nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3•9H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 98%), citric acid (C6H8O7, Sigma Aldrich, 99.5%), and ethylene glycol (C2H6O2, Sigma Aldrich, 99.8%). Depending on the substitution series, one of the following rare earth nitrates was incorporated: gadolinium nitrate hexahydrate (Gd(NO3)3•6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%), samarium nitrate hexahydrate (Sm(NO3)3•6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%), neodymium nitrate hexahydrate (Nd(NO3)3•6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%), praseodymium nitrate hexahydrate (Pr(NO3)3•6H2O, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%), or lanthanum nitrate hexahydrate (La(NO3)3•6H2O, Fluka, 99%). The formation of substituted hexaferrites followed the reaction scheme shown in Eq. (1). (1 − x) Sr(NO3)2 + (x)RE(NO3)3 + 12 Fe(NO3)3 →Sr1− x RExFe12O19 + (38 + x)NO2 ↑ + (9.5 + 0.5x)O2 ↑ (1) The precursor salts were carefully weighed in stoichiometric proportions required to obtain 1.0 g of hexaferrite powder for each sample. Reagent quantities were calculated considering the targeted stoichiometry of the respective substituted hexaferrites. Moreover, a 3 wt% excess of rare earth nitrate was added to compensate for potential material loss during the sintering process [18]. The quantities of the rare earth precursors used for the synthesis of the corresponding hexaferrite samples are listed in Table 1. The synthesis process involved dissolving stoichiometric amounts of nitrate salts in 20 mL of deionized water under magnetic agitation. Subsequently, ethylene glycol and citric acid were added in a 4:1 M ratio, together with an additional 20 mL of deionized water. The mixture was first heated to 85 °C to remove excess water and subsequently raised to 100 °C to promote the polyesterification reaction. The resulting resin for each composition was subjected to thermal treatment at 380 °C for 40 min, followed by manual grinding in an agate mortar. Finally, the obtained powders were calcined in air at 1100 °C for 4 h and allowed to cool down gradually inside the furnace.
Comment: Magnetic room temperature (no number given). Pechini powders calcined 1100 C/4 h in air. Ms = M at 15 kOe (Section 3.5).

Synthesis_Procedure: So we used citrate-nitrate gel combustion method to obtain aluminum-substituted barium hexaferrite BaAl4Fe8O19. Barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2, analytical grade), aluminum nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO3)3⋅9H2O, chemically pure), iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, pure), citric acid monohydrate (C6H8O7⋅H2O, pure), and 25 wt.% aqueous ammonia (NH4OH(aq), analytical grade) were used. This approach involved weighing nitrates in stoichiometric proportions. Citric acid was weighed at a rate of 3 moles of acid per 1 mol of total nitrates. The weighed portions were dissolved in a minimal amount of water, and the resulting solutions were mixed in a porcelain dish. After 15 min of room temperature stirring, the mixture was neutralized by adding an aqueous ammonia solution to a pH of 8 (monitored using universal indicator paper). The solution was then slowly evaporated in a boiling water bath until a honey-like mass was obtained. The resulting honey-like mass is presumably a mixture of barium, iron, and aluminum nitrates, ammonium citrate, and residual water. A porcelain cup containing the resulting mass was heated in a muffle furnace. During heating, final dehydration and thermal decomposition of the ammonium citrate and nitrates occur. Oxygen formed during the decomposition of the nitrates oxidizes the citric acid. Heating releases a large amount of gases, causing the mass to foam. Preliminary studies showed that heating should be done slowly, as rapid heating (over 1–2 h) causes the mass to swell excessively and may fall out of the cup. Therefore, the following heating program was used: 1) heating for 1 h to 100 °C; 2) holding for 2 h at 100 °C; 3) heating for 2 h to 150 °C; 4) holding for 2 h at 150 °C; 5) heating for 2 h to 200 °C; 6) holding for 2 h at 200 °C; cooling along with the furnace. This process resulted in the formation of a bulk xerogel. The xerogel was thoroughly ground and transferred to a porcelain crucible. To oxidize the residual carbon, the xerogel was heated in a muffle furnace at 500 °C for 6 h. The resulting material was ferritized in a corundum crucible. The method was firstly tested on pure barium hexaferrite. Ferritization temperature was selected as the variable parameter. X-ray phase analysis showed that holding the material at 900 °C for 4 h was sufficient for complete ferritization of BaFe12O19. Given that a higher sintering temperature is a priori required to obtain BaAl4Fe8O19, it was decided to ferritize it at 1100 °C for 4 h.

Sm doped barium hexaferrite structures were synthesized with chemical formula Ba1-xSmxFe12O19 (x = 0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.10, 0.20) via sol–gel auto-combustion method. The flow chart was shown in Fig. 2. Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3•9H2O and Sm(NO3)3•6H2O were dissolved in deionized water under continuous stirring at room temperature. The mixture was continuously stirred at room temperature to obtain homogenous solution. Then, the resulting mixture was placed into an oven and dried at 80 °C to evaporate water. The obtained viscous gel was subjected to a self-combustion reaction in an oven at 200 °C. The obtained powder was thoroughly ground and calcined in a muffle furnace at 1100 °C with a heating rate of 5 °C/min, which maintained for 5 h to obtain the final product.

The resulting mixture was continuously stirred to ensure complete dissolution and uniform distribution of the precursor ions. To regulate the gelation process and control the chemical environment, the pH of the solution was carefully adjusted to 8 by the gradual addition of ammonia solution. Upon sustained heating and stirring, the metal ions interacted with the complexing agent, initiating gel formation. This was followed by a self-propagating exothermic reaction within the gel, leading to spontaneous combustion and the formation of a fine, porous powder. The obtained powder was then calcined in a muffle furnace at 1200 °C for 6 h to enhance crystallinity, phase purity, and thermal stability of the hexaferrite phase.

Synthesis_Procedure: Microcrystalline samples of strontium M-type hexaferrite SrFe12-xInxO19 (with doping levels x = 1.7, 1.8 and 2.0 Indium atoms per formula unit (f.u.)) were synthesized via the citrate gel combustion method using nitrates Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, In(NO3)3⋅3H2O, (NH4)OH and C6H8O7 (all Sigma-Aldrich, technical grade, purity >98 %) as precursors. The as-synthesized powders were subsequently annealed at 1200 °C for 1 h in an air atmosphere. For nanoparticle production the SrFe12-xInxO19 microcrystalline powders were subjected to high-energy ball milling using a planetary ball mill PM 400 (Retsch, Germany) at a rotational speed of 400 rpm for 50 h. The milling medium comprised 1-octadecene with oleic acid (OA) added as a surfactant. A powder-to-ball mass ratio of 1:10 was maintained. Following milling, the particles were washed to remove residual 1-octadecene and transferred into dichloromethane (DCM). Ultrasonic homogenization was then performed to disrupt particle agglomerates. Subsequently, the particles were coated with hydrophilic biocompatible Pluronic F-127 copolymer to enable aqueous stabilization. For coating, powder suspensions were prepared in toluene. An aqueous solution of Pluronic F-127 was then introduced to the toluene suspensions. An emulsion was formed via ultrasonic homogenization. This emulsion was centrifuged, resulting in phase separation where the toluene migrated to form the upper phase. The toluene phase was carefully decanted and replaced with deionized water with subsequent sonication until a homogeneous sol is formed. After that the final hydrophilized nanoparticles were collected by centrifugation.

Synthesis_Procedure: Ba-Zn hexaferrite nanoparticles were prepared by a sol-gel auto combustion process, which is an energy-saving process, requires low annealing temperatures to enhance crystal growth or particle size, and improves composition purity, also synthesizes ultrafine nano-sized particles with specific surface area, physicochemical properties, and fast reaction rate. The solutions (300 ml) contain stoichiometric quantities of Ba(NO3)2 .6H2O, Fe(NO3)2 .9H2O, and Zn(NO3)2 .6H2O. It was prepared by weighing the compositional atomic ratios and mixed under magnetic stirring for 30 min to get the precursor sol. For promoting the interaction of electronegative oxygen ions and electropositive ions, citric acid was selected as a chelating agent and also responsible for the binding of Zn2+ , Ba2+, and Fe3+ cations with anions (citrate 2− and citrate3− ), metal nitrate was surpassed during precipitation and water removal [32], [33]. Solution of citric acid (C6H8O7 .H2O) prepared in 300 ml of deionized water was dissolved into the mixture of nitrates under constant stirring. The molar ratio of metal ions to citric acid was kept 1:1. To get a pH of 7, a solution of ammonium hydroxide was added drop by drop to the resulting mixture, followed by a 5-hour heating process at 300 °C until the solvent completely evaporated. The remaining viscous gel of dark brown color was self-ignited and spread and swelled out of the container at the end. After the precursors are completely decomposed, a brown powder is formed. Finally, powder calcination is performed at 900o C for 7 hours. Using a mortar and pestle, a finely grind powder of Ba-Zn nanoparticles was obtained with a distinct phase [34], [35].

The concentration was selected to provide sufficient green compact strength and minimize drying cracks during pellet preparation. Although higher binder levels may promote porosity, the subsequent calcination at 1260 °C ensures complete removal of the organic phase, resulting in dense microstructures with well-developed grains. The mixture was then pressed into pellets and calcined at 1260 °C in a muffle furnace to achieve the desired magnetoplumbite phase. Following calcination, the pellets underwent crushing and grinding. To obtain fine and uniform particles, the powder was processed through wet ball milling in a rolling mill for a duration of 20 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Strontium chloride (SrCl2.6H2O), anhydrous Ferric chloride (FeCl3), Zinc nitrate Zn(NO3)2, diethylene glycol and sodium hydroxide were commercially purchased from Merck, India. Analytical grade chemicals were used without further purification all through the experiments. Zinc doped strontium ferrite metacomposites were synthesised by a facile route, schematically shown in Fig. 2. The processes are explained under this section. Hydrothermal method was used to prepare the samples. In this procedure, the nanostructured Sr1-xZnxFe12O19 (Sr and Fe ratio 1:8) with x fraction varying as 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 were prepared by dissolving appropriate amount of precursors like SrCl2.6H2O and anhydrous FeCl3 and Zn(NO3)2.6H2O were mixed with small amount of deionized water to form a homogeneous solution. This solution was kept under magnetic stirring with subsequent addition of ethylene glycol as surfactant at room temperature [13]. Afterwards, freshly prepared saturated sodium hydroxide solution was added to the mixture to adjust the pH to 12, and the whole mixture solution were continuously stirred for 45 min until a homogeneous solution is obtained. This was then poured into a 100 ml Teflon beaker and placed inside a hydrothermal autoclave and heated for 20 h at 180 °C. Finally, it was allowed to cool to room temperature naturally. Then, the solid powder was separated and washed with distilled water and dried. This dried powder was then heat treated at 900 °C for 10 h in a furnace to obtain the final product. Final products of Sr1-xZnxFe12O19 (x = 0–0.5, step of 0.1) samples such as SrFe12O19, Sr0.9Zn0.1Fe12O19, Sr0.8Zn0.2Fe12O19, Sr0.7Zn0.3Fe12O19, Sr0.6Zn0.4Fe12O19, and Sr0.5Zn0.5Fe12O19are labelled as SF, SZ1, SZ2, SZ3, SZ4 and SZ5, respectively.

Synthesis_Procedure: Polycrystalline samples of BaFe12-xAxO19 (x = 0.1 and A = Ru4+ or Re4+) and BaFe12-xM2xO19 (x = 0.05; and M = (Ru4+, Re4+)) were prepared using the solid-state reaction method. The starting powders of BaCO3, Fe2O3, RuO2, and ReO2 with a purity > 98 % (Sigma-AldrichBrazil), were mixed in the desired stoichiometry. The stoichiometric mixtures were milled for 8 h to obtain finer particles and then calcined in air at 1000 °C for 8 h with a 20°C/min heating rate. The calcined powders were ground for 4 h and immediately sieved. After that, some amounts of the powders were pressed at 2.6 ton/cm2 in a 10 mm diameter disk-shaped samples and sintered at 1100 °C for 4 h, with a 10°C/min heating rate. Synthesis_Procedure: Sol-gel method was adapted to prepare M-type barium hexaferrite samples by considering analytical grade Ba(NO3)2 and Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O as starting materials in stoichiometric ratios and dissolved in distilled water separately. These solutions were added into a beaker and while stirring on a hot plate, the citric acid solution was prepared separately by taking in the ratio of 1:1.2 w.r.t metal ion. Using a separating funnel with constant stirring the citric acid solution was added drop wise to the resultant solution and pH was maintained between 6.5 and 7.0 by adding ammonia solution. This solution was heated on a hot plate (90 °C) till the solution reached to one third of its value and later ethylene glycol was added in the ratio of 1: 2 and stirred for 30 min. The heating is continued and burns automatically giving rise to a foamy brown mass with the evaluation of gases. The mass is collected and grounded for 1 hr in an agate mortar and calcined at 700 °C/3h and the powders were made into circular pellets of 10 mm diameter. The pellets were sintered in a microwave furnace with a soaking time of 30 min by sintering at four different temperatures i.e., 750 °C, 850 °C, 950 °C & 1050 °C and cooled to room temperature.

Synthesis_Procedure: Here, the sol-gel approach was chosen, as the technique yields particles that are finer in size [20,27]. In sol-gel processes, nitrates or oxides are typically employed as precursors. Every precursor was dissolved in double distilled water (DDW). To synthesize SrFe12O19, the precursors analytical grade Strontium Nitrate (Sr(NO3)2) (98 % SRL) and Ferric nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O) (98 % Sigma-Aldrich) were chosen. The reaction is, Sr(NO3)2 + Fe(NO3)3.9H2O→SrFe12O19 + H2O + N2 + O2 Additionally, a few other chemicals were added along with them that serve as secondary reagents. Citric acid (C6H8O7.H2O) (99.5 % SigmaAldrich), being a chelating agent, acts as a fuel thereby enhancing the rate of reaction for the synthesis of hexaferrite [33]. With that being said, it has to be noted that a complex precursor solution was produced when citric acid combined with metal ions, facilitating the production of finer particles and accurate stoichiometry [34]. The molar ratio of citric acid: metal ion was 1:1. Subsequently, ethylene glycol, C2H6O2(99.8 % Sigma-Aldrich), was mixed into the solution as a gelation agent. This promotes the formation of uniform and viscous gel, which guarantees a homogenous distribution of nanoparticles [35]. Ammonia solution NH4OH (30 % Sigma-Aldrich), serves as a pH buffer by maintaining the pH of the solution at a slightly basic level, which is required for producing the desired hexaferrite phase [28,34]. The solution was mixed and heated at 90 °C till the gel formation and raised to 150 °C till they undergo auto-combustion yielding SrFe12O19 and BaFe12O19 powders respectively. Analytical grade Barium Nitrate (Ba(NO3)2) (99 SRL) and Ferric nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O) (98 % Sigma-Aldrich) were opted as primary reagents for BaFe12O19 synthesis. Ba(NO3)2 + Fe(NO3)3.9H2O→BaFe12O19 + H2O + N2 + O2 The same procedures were followed for the reaction that gives out Barium hexaferrite. Each material was divided into 2 batches, ground well using a mortar and pestle, and compressed into a rectangular plate using a hydraulic press. For conventional sintering, both SrFe12O19 and BaFe12O19 powders were pre-sintered at 800 °C for 3 h followed by a final sintering at 1150 °C for 2 h in a conventional box furnace. A heating rate of 5 °C/min was maintained during the process. In the case of microwave sintering, plates were pre-sintered at 800 °C for 20 min and then annealed at 1150 °C for 20 min in a microwave furnace at a rate of 30 °C/min. It has been reported that sintering at 1000 °C or below results in samples with incomplete crystallization and smaller grain size. On the other side, temperatures beyond 1300 °C cause thermal decomposition and the formation of unnecessary secondary phases. A longer period is observed to cause the melting of the materials and thermal runaways. Hence, the time period of 20 min for microwave sintering was adopted [25]. The plate was crushed, ground again to powders after pre-sintering, and remoulded into the same shape before going through the final sintering in each case to ensure uniform particle size distribution and enhance mechanical properties. The synthesis process was repeated with temperature optimization until consistent powder yields were achieved from the same amount of precursors, and reproducible density was confirmed through XRD analysis.

In the first step, high-purity BaCO3 (99.8 %), Fe2O3 (99.5 %), CuO (99 %), and SnO2 (99.9 %) were used as raw materials. In the second step, the weighed powders were placed into a ball milling jar, with deionized water added for wetting. The mixture was then subjected to planetary ball milling at a rotational speed of 250 rpm for 12 h to ensure uniformity. In the seventh step, the ground powder was sieved using a dual-layer mesh screen, with an upper mesh of 120 and a lower mesh of 80, to obtain granulated sample powders. In the eighth step, the powder retained on the 80-mesh sieve was selected and pressed into disc-shaped samples under a pressure of 4 MPa. In the ninth step, the disc-shaped samples were sintered in a muffle furnace at 1100 °C for 6 h, followed by gradual cooling to room temperature under ambient air conditions.

These pellets were sintered at 1050 °C, 1150 °C, 1250 °C and 1300 °C for 2 h in a conventional resistive heating furnace with a heating rate of 1 °C/min. Synthesis_Procedure: The sol–gel auto-combustion method is a versatile and effective technique for synthesizing ferrite nanoparticles, renowned for its simplicity and efficiency [23]. First of all, the metal salt solution was prepared by mixing various nitrate salts, including Ba(NO3)2.3H2O, Fe(NO3)3.9H2O, Pr(NO3)3.6H2O, and Al(NO3)3.9H2O, combined with anhydrous citric acid, ethylene glycol, and ammonia solution. The 0.02 mol solution was prepared using stoichiometric amounts as given in Table S1. These components are dissolved in 20–25 ml of double-distilled water through continuous stirring to achieve a clear, homogeneous solution. Citric acid plays a crucial role as a chelating agent by forming stable complexes with metal ions to prevent hydroxylation and ensure uniform chemical composition [24]. On the other hand, water-soluble salts function as low-temperature oxidizers facilitating the initial stages of the reaction. A crucial step that influences the size and properties of the resulting nanoparticles is the adjustment of the pH of the solution in the range of 7–8 using ammonia. Ethylene glycol acts as a surfactant when introduced into the mixture at a temperature of 80°C [25]. This addition is a key in preventing the agglomeration of nanoparticles and controlling the viscosity of the solution which helps in managing the cation exchange rates and forming a uniform polymer network. This surfactant also aids in enhancing heat evolution and lowering the temperature needed for ignition which is necessary for promoting the development of single-phase hexaferrite. The resulting powder is subjected to calcination at a temperature of 1050 °C for 4 h after the initial reaction. This hightemperature treatment ensures the formation of the desired crystalline structure. Various steps involved in the synthesis of Ba0.5Pr0.5Fe12-xAlxO19 hexaferrites by the sol–gel method are given in Fig. 1.

Synthesis_Procedure: Analytical-grade chemicals, such as Barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2), Strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2), Ferric nitrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O), and Ruthenium chloride (RuCl3⋅xH2O), were purchased from Sigma Aldrich and used for synthesis purpose without further purification. Citric acid (C6H8O7, 98 %) was utilized as a combustion agent, and ammonia solution (NH4OH, 25 %) was used to maintain a pH level of 7. The Ba0.5Sr0.5RuxFe12-xO19 (0.00≤x ≤ 0.20) samples were synthesized using the sol-gel auto-combustion method. In a typical synthesis, stoichiometric amounts of Ba(NO3)2, Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and RuCl3⋅xH2O were dissolved in deionized water under constant stirring to become a homogenous aqueous solution. The Citric acid was used to add in a molar ratio of 1:2 with respect to the total metal ions to act as a chelating and combustion agent. The mixture was heated to a temperature of 80 °C with constant stirring until a viscous gel was formed. To adjust the pH of the solution to 7, the ammonia solution was added slowly in a dropwise manner, ensuring optimal conditions for gelation. The gel was then subjected to further heating until self-ignition occurred, resulting in a fluffy precursor powder. This precursor powder was ground into a fine powder using an agate mortar and pestle and calcined at 1100 °C for 4 h in a muffle furnace to produce the final hexaferrite powder phase.

Synthesis_Procedure: All the starting reagents of the high-purity analytical grade (Merck Co., Germany) were utilized to synthesize BaMNPs. Appropriate amounts of iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O; 99.9 %) and barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2; 99.9 %) were employed as metallic cation substances. Distilled water was used as a solvent. Additionally, sodium hydroxide (NaOH; 25 %) and albumin (C6H8N2O4; 99 %) were used as a reduction agent and natural additives, respectively. BaMNPs were fabricated using the co-precipitation method. Fig. 1 depicts the schematic of the main six steps involved in the synthesis process employed in this study. The synthesized nanoparticles are denoted as A1 to A9. First, the stoichiometric (or a nonstoichiometric) molar ratio of iron to barium cations and different amounts of albumin were dissolved in distilled water at room temperature to form a homogeneous solution. The solution was heated to 80 °C under constant stirring, and NaOH solution was added dropwise to adjust the pH to 11. NaOH as a mineralizer subsequently led to the precipitation of the nanoparticles. Following this stage, continuous magnetic stirring at a constant speed and heating for 1 h completed the process. The precipitates were washed with distilled water through several cycles to obtain a neutral pH of approximately 7 and remove any remaining NaOH. The synthesized nanoparticles were filtered and dried at 80 °C for 4 hours in an electric oven. Finally, the nanoparticles were calcined at 900 °C for 4 h in an air atmosphere, resulting in the formation of a crystallized structure.

Synthesis_Procedure: All the starting reagents of the high-purity analytical grade (Merck Co., Germany) were utilized to synthesize BaMNPs. Appropriate amounts of iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O; 99.9 %) and barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2; 99.9 %) were employed as metallic cation substances. Distilled water was used as a solvent. Additionally, sodium hydroxide (NaOH; 25 %) and albumin (C6H8N2O4; 99 %) were used as a reduction agent and natural additives, respectively. BaMNPs were fabricated using the co-precipitation method. Fig. 1 depicts the schematic of the main six steps involved in the synthesis process employed in this study. The synthesized nanoparticles are denoted as A1 to A9. First, the stoichiometric (or a nonstoichiometric) molar ratio of iron to barium cations and different amounts of albumin were dissolved in distilled water at room temperature to form a homogeneous solution. The solution was heated to 80 °C under constant stirring, and NaOH solution was added dropwise to adjust the pH to 11. NaOH as a mineralizer subsequently led to the precipitation of the nanoparticles. Following this stage, continuous magnetic stirring at a constant speed and heating for 1 h completed the process. The precipitates were washed with distilled water through several cycles to obtain a neutral pH of approximately 7 and remove any remaining NaOH. The synthesized nanoparticles were filtered and dried at 80 °C for 4 hours in an electric oven. Finally, the nanoparticles were calcined at 900 °C for 4 h in an air atmosphere, resulting in the formation of a crystallized structure.
