Synthesis_Procedure: Using the sol–gel self-ignition method, Ba0.3Sr0.3Ca0.4Al0.5SmxFe11.50-xO19 (x = 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75), were synthesized. For the synthesis, A.R. grade chemicals from Sigma-Aldrich with > 99 % purity were used, such as citric acid (C6H8O7⋅H2O) and the nitrates of Ba, Sr, Ca, Al, Sm, and Fe, specifically Ba(NO3)2, Sr(NO3)2, Ca (NO3)3⋅4H2O, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and Sm(NO3)⋅6H2O. To create the clear suspension, double-distilled water was used to dissolve the molar quantities of the compounds through stoichiometry. The fuel, which consisted of metal nitrates and citric acid, was at a 3:1 ratio. To keep the pH of the solution at 7, the ammonia solution was added drop by drop. Using a magnetic stirrer-heater, the neutralized nitrate-citrate aqueous solution was heated (to 100 °C) and stirred continuously. A viscous gel with a darker color is the end result of an hour of continuous evaporation. When the gel is heated, all of its water molecules evaporate, causing it to self-proliferate and produce thick, colorful vapors. The selfpropagation process takes about two minutes to produce black ash, which is then thoroughly mixed in an agate mortar to create a uniform powder. High temperatures are necessary for hexaferrites to completely develop an appropriate crystal structure and to eliminate carbonates. By preventing secondary phases that can impair magnetic performance, the high calcination temperature guarantees the full reaction between iron oxide and the alkaline earth metal oxide. Fine, well-crystallized particles that are appropriate for sintering or other processing are produced by properly calcining at 1100 °C [51–53]. Hexaferrite is the result of sintering the powder for four hours at 1100 degrees Celsius. Hexaferrite powder samples were used for magnetic property assessment and structural clarification.

Synthesis_Procedure: (Ba(NO3)2, 99 %), Ferric nitrate (Fe(NO3)3, 98 %), Lanthanum Nitrate (La(NO3)3 (99.95 %), Oxalic acid (C2H2O4)(98 %), D-Galactose (C6H12O6, 98 %), and Ethylene glycol (C2H6O2) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Acetone (99.5 %) was used to clean all glassware used in this experiment. Pure distilled water wa s used for sample preparation. The synthesis of BaFe12-xLaxO19 nanoparticles begins with the preparation of metal nitrate solutions. Ferric nitrate (Fe(NO3)3) is dissolved in 20 ml of distilled water and stirred for 30 min, while barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2) and lanthanum nitrate (La(NO3)3) solutions (with varying concentrations, x = 0.00 to 0.05) are prepared separately and stirred for 15 min each. These solutions are gradually combined while stirring continuously to ensure a homogeneous metal cation mixture. For gel formation, 4 ml of D-galactose is dissolved in deionized water, stirred for 30 min, and slowly added to the metal nitrate mixture. After 15 min,1 ml of ethylene glycol is introduced, followed by the dissolution of 1 g of oxalic acid in a small volume of distilled water. This solution is stirred for 30 min and added dropwise to the ferric nitrate solution at 80 °C, with continuous stirring until a gel forms, indicating the development of a three-dimensional network. The total time required for gel formation is 3 h. All these experiments are performed at room temperature.

Synthesis_Procedure: The BaFe12-xCrxO19 and BaFe12-xAlxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.4) powders were prepared by hydrothermal synthesis followed by annealing. The solutions were prepared with the expectation that in the final volume (80 ml) the total concentration of Fe3+ and Al3+ (or Cr3+) ions would be 0.25 M, the (Fe3++Al3+)/Ba2+ or (Fe3++Cr3+)/ Ba2+ ratios would be 9, and the OH–/NO–3 ratio would be 2.5. After that, the resulting mixture was placed into a 100 ml Teflon vessel, sealed in autoclave, and placed in a muffle furnace. The autoclave was slowly heated to 180 °C for 2 h and kept at this temperature for 4 h. Precipitate formed was washed in distilled water several times and dried at 90 °C overnight. The dry residue was ground in a mortar and annealed in a muffle furnace in air. The heating rate was 15° /min, the final temperature was 900 °C, and the annealing time was 1 h. Next, powders were washed in 10-% HCl to remove possible side phases (e.g. BaCO3 and BaFe2O4).

Synthesis_Procedure: Dissolve 8.5 g (0.00175 mol) of ferric nitrate (Fe(NO3)3) in 20 ml of DI water and stir until completely dissolved. Separately, dissolve 0.45 g (0.0019 mol) of barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2) in 4 ml of DI water. Then prepare samarium nitrate (Sm(NO3)3) solutions with varying concentrations (x = 0.00, 0.01 (0.00179 mol), 0.02 (0.0034 mol), 0.03(0.0052 mol), 0.04 (0.071 mol), 0.05g (0.087 mol)). Slowly pour the ferric nitrate solution and the prepared samarium nitrate solutions into the barium nitrate solution while stirring constantly to ensure the metal cations mix well. Then dissolve D-Galactose 4.1g (0.027mol) in a minimal amount of DI water, continue stirring for 30 min, then add this solution drop by drop to the metal nitrate mixture with continuous stirring for homogeneous mixing. Then, add 1 ml (0.0144 mol) of ethylene glycol and stir for an additional 30 min; ethylene glycol acts as a chelating agent. Also dissolve 1 g (0.0079 mol) of oxalic acid in a small amount of DI water and add this solution dropwise to the mixture while stirring continuously. Stir until a visible gel form which indicates the development of a three-dimensional network, then heat the mixture to 60–80 °C with continuous stir. After stirring for 3 h, transfer the sticky gel to a crucible and place it in a hot-air oven preheated to 120 °C and dried for 24 h. Then grind the gel into a fine powder using a mortar and pestle. Finally, the powder was calcined to 800 °C to transform the precursor into the desired phase of BHF for further processing.

Synthesis_Procedure: The barium hexaferrite powders were prepared by hydrothermal synthesis. The precursor for synthesis of pure BaFe12O19 was a mixture of a 60 ml of aqueous salt solution of iron nitrate nonahydrate Fe (NO3)3⋅9H2O (8.08 g) and barium nitrate Ba(NO3)2 (0.58 g) with a 15 ml of aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide NaOH (6.44 g). The solutions were prepared with the expectation that the Fe3+/Ba2+ ratio would be 9, and the OH–/NO–3 ratio would be 2.5 [36]. For the doped ferrites Cr (NO3)3⋅9H2O (0.32 g), Ni(NO3)2⋅6H2O (0.23 g), Co(NO3)2⋅6H2O (0.23 g) or MnCl2⋅4H2O (0.158 g) were added to the salt solution before mixing with alkali. The amount of these salts corresponds to 4 % mol. of the amount of iron nitrate. After that, the resulting mixture was placed into a 100 ml PPL vessel, sealed, and placed in an oven. The autoclave was slowly heated to 180 °C for 2 h and kept at this temperature for 4 h. The precipitates obtained were washed with distilled water several times and separated from the liquid in a centrifuge.

Synthesis_Procedure: The Ba0.5Sr0.5Al0.5Fe11.5-xPrxO19(0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.15) nanoparticles were synthesized via the sol–gel auto-combustion method using high-purity reagents, including praseodymium nitrate (Pr(NO3)3⋅6H2O)(SigmaAldrich, 99 %), ferric nitrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O) (Sigma-Aldrich, 98 %), strontium nitrate (Sr(NO3)2) (Sigma-Aldrich, 99 %), barium nitrate (Ba (NO3)2) (Sigma-Aldrich, 99 %), aluminum nitrate (Al(NO3)3)(SigmaAldrich, 99 %), citric acid (Riedel-Dehaen, >99.5 %), and ammonia (Riedel, 33 %). (Table S1) Initially, metal salts were dissolved in deionized water to prepare the metal nitrate solution. Citric acid was then dissolved separately and added to this solution in a molar ratio of 1:1 (citric acid to metal ions), resulting in a homogeneous mixture. Ammonia (25 %) was progressively added to the solution to adjust the pH to approximately 7, yielding a stable final solution. The solution was stirred continuously at 90 °C until it condensed into a homogeneous, viscous liquid. This gel-like solution was dried in an oven at 105 °C to obtain a thick gel. Subsequently, the gel underwent thermal treatment in an electric furnace, where it experienced a self-propagating combustion process, resulting in the formation of a fluffy bulky powder. The powder was finely ground with a pestle and mortar to achieve a uniform particle size. Finally, the resulting fine powder was sintered at 1050 °C for 3 h to enhance the crystallinity and structural integrity of the hexaferrite phase. Synthesis_Procedure: The reaction for obtaining hexaferrite BaFe12O19 by the method of self-propagating high-temperature synthesis is as follows: BaO2 + 3 Fe2O3 + 6 Fe + 4 O2 → BaFe12O19 (1) The oxidizing agent in the reaction is O2, one part of which is introduced into the charge in a solid state (as part of BaO2 and Fe2O3), and the other part enters by filtration from the external environment. Thus, the mechanism of interaction of reagents combines the features of gasless and filtration combustion [25]. Barium peroxide contains significantly more labile oxygen than the oxides and carbonates used in solid-phase synthesis, so its use in ferrite formation reactions is more advantageous and results in the absence of contamination, in particular with carbon. During the oxidation of free iron, heat is released, which provides a self-sustaining synthesis mechanism. Barium peroxide BaO2 (>99.9 %), iron (III) oxide Fe2O3 (>99 %), and carbonyl iron powder (R10 brand) were used as initial reagents. The powders were dried at a temperature of 100 °C for 3 h. After this, the initial components were dosed on analytical balances and mixed by grinding in an agate mortar. The resulting mixture of components weighing 20 g was poured into a reactor – a horizontally located quartz tube, hermetically sealed at both ends with metal lids. The lids are equipped with special openings designed for the supply and removal of oxygen to the reaction mixture through a flowmeter, as well as the introduction of a chromel–alumel thermocouple and an electric nichrome coil to initiate the combustion process. The synthesis of substances was carried out in an oxygen flow, maintaining a given pressure using a manometer. The flow rate and pressure in the reactor were 0.7 m3/h and 12 kPa, respectively. The maximum combustion temperature was 1000 °C. The combustion temperature was chosen based on the known literature data [13]. The speed of reaching the maximum combustion temperature was 140 °C/s. The duration of combustion at this temperature was 1 min. Then the SHS products were ground in an agate mortar, pressed under a pressure of 100 MPa and placed in a muffle furnace for annealing. Ferritization was carried out in an air atmosphere at temperature range of 1000–1250 °C for 2 h. Then the ceramic ferrites were ground in a ball mill with a mass ratio of ceramics to grinding bodies of 1:10 for 5 h. The following designations were used for BaFe12O19 hexaferrites: No. 1 – without annealing, No. 2 – 1000 °C, No. 3 – 1100 °C, No. 4 – 1200 °C, No. 5 – 1250 °C.

Synthesis_Procedure: All the precursors of AR grade ( > 98%), including the ferric nitrate (SimSon company), cobalt nitrate (SimSon company), barium nitrate (Merck company), and citric acid (SimSon company), are used to fabricate the Ba1-xCoxFe12O19 (x = 0.2–0.6) hexaferrites. Furthermore, the ammonia solution (from SimSon company) and ethylene glycol (Ramkem company) are used to neutralised the solution and for the gel formation. The SGC technique is utilised to fabricate the Ba1-xCoxFe12O19 (x = 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6) hexaferrite nanoparticles. In this technique, the barium, cobalt, and iron nitrates are used as reagents and a citric acid solution is used as fuel. Firstly, the solution of citric acid and all nitrates dissolved in distilled water individually and stirred for two hours at room temperature using a magnetic stirrer with a heated plate until it turns to the transparent solution, signifying full dissolution. When the solution becomes clear, add the nitrate solution and stir atleast for 30 min. With continuous stirring, the concentrated NH4OH solution is added to the solution drop by drop until the pH reaches to 7.0. Once the pH has been stabilised, the ethylene glycol is added to the solution to initiate the gel formation. The resultant solution is stirred at 100 °C for one hour. Synthesis_Procedure: The ceramic sample synthesis procedure for BaZnZrFe10O19 (BZFO) and BaFe12O19 (BFO) is solid state reaction technique, similar to the approach used by Swati et al. [41]. For BFO sample barium carbonate (BaCO3), iron oxide (Fe2O3) and for BZFO sample barium carbonate (BaCO3), iron oxide (Fe2O3), zinc oxide (ZnO) and zirconium dioxide (ZrO2) were used as raw materials. The general chemical reactions involved in the synthesis of BFO and BZFO samples at 1200 °C temperature are as follows. 1. BaCO3 + 6Fe2O3 → BaFe12O19 + CO2 2. BaCO3 + 5Fe2O3 + ZnO + ZrO2 → BaZnZrFe10O19 + CO2 These raw materials were weighed stoichiometrically. The weighed chemicals were ball milled using 20 zirconia balls in the acetone medium for 24 h. The wet mixture for both types (BFO & BZFO) were air dried and then calcined for 6 h between 900 °C and 1200 °C using muffle furnace. The calcined samples were ground using motar and pestle to obtain fine powder. This ground powder was used for XRD measurements. 6 wt% polyvinyl alcohol binding material was added to the grounded powders for making pellets for FESEM, magnetic and microwave studies. PVA mixed powders were hydraulically pressed into two different sized a) 22.86 mm × 10.16 mm rectangular pellets for X-band microwave studies at 1.5 ton pressure and b) 10 mm diameter and 1.5 mm thick pellets pressed at 6 ton pressure for FESEM and magnetic measurements. PVA was eliminated by reheating the pellets at 1000 °C for three hours.

Synthesis_Procedure: The samples were fabricated by sol–gel auto-combustion, a technique that combines the standard sol–gel process with auto-ignition combustion. Iron and barium nitrate precursors, along with citric acid, acted as chelating agents, and were utilized in analytical purity. Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Ba(NO3)2, Al(NO3)3·9H2O, and Ga(NO3)3 were dissolved in deionized water in the molar ratio corresponding to BaAlxGaxFe12-2xO19, yielding a homogeneous and transparent sol. As a chelating agent, citric acid underwent ionization and formed chelates with Fe3+ and Ba2+ ions. The stoichiometric ratio of citric acid to metal nitrate was set at 1:1. A neutral pH solution was prepared by controlling the addition of ethylenediamine (C2H8N2) to the mixture of citric acid and metal nitrate. After 1 h of incubation in the water bath at 80°C, the solution remained clear, demonstrating that Fe3+ and Ba2+ had effectively formed citrate complexes. Upon heating, the viscosity of citrate solutions increased as water evaporated, and eventually the brown gel formed. The gel then self-ignited in an auto-combustion process, leaving behind fluffy powder residues after complete burning. After that, the powder underwent thermal treatment at 1100°C for 2 h in a sintering furnace to obtain the test samples.

Initially, stoichiometric quantities of nitrates were mixed in 100 mL deionized water and stirred for 15 min on a hot plate under magnetic stirring. These dried samples were manually crushed into a fine powder using a mortar and pestle, and then annealed for 12 h at 1000 °C. The annealed powders were compressed under a compaction pressure of 5 tons per cm2 using a hydraulic press to produce pellets. Finally, the pelletized samples were sintered for 6 h at 1200 °C in a furnace.

The ball, material, and water ratio is 20:1:1, and the ball mill speed is 95 r/min for 11 h. The slurry was pressed into 25 mm by a 23 t semiautomatic powder magnetic field forming machine, and 25 mm round billet was put in a muffle furnace at 1220 °C, sintered for 5 h [20,21], and then naturally cooled. Next, the samples were calcined at 1300 ºC for 6 hours to ensure the formation of M-type hexaferrite phase. Finally, the pellets were sintered at 1300 ºC for 6 hours.

Synthesis_Procedure: Leaves of Tecomastans (yellow bell) plant were collected from the Gujarat University campus, Ahmedabad, India and were washed twice with tap water followed by distilled water and then air dried for 2 h, 30g of leaves chopped roughly were taken in 200 ml of double distilled water and heated on a hot plate at 80 °C for 45 min. Sr0⋅8Ce0⋅2Fe12-xAlxO19 (x = 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, and 1.00) ferrites were prepared using a modified sol-gel auto combustion technique in the presence of leaf extract of Tecomastans (yellow bell) plant. All metal nitrates (strontium nitrate anhydrous Sr(NO3)2 (99.0 % pure, HPLC), cerium(III) nitrate hexahydrate Ce(NO3)3 • 6H2O (99.0 % pure, Sigma Aldrich), iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate Fe(NO3)3 • 9H2O (≥ 99.0 % pure, HPLC), aluminium nitrate nonahydrate Al(NO3)2 • 9H2O (98.5 % pure, HPLC)) were taken in stoichiometric amounts and dissolved one by one in 100 ml double distilled water and then mixed using a magnetic stirrer. Yellow bell leaves extract of 140 ml was added dropwise into nitrate solution and then ammonia solution (25 % w/v) was added until pH adjusted to 7.0. This homogeneous solution was heated at 100 °C on a sand bath for ~3 h. After evaporation of the water from the solution, it was converted into a gel. Further heating of the gel gave dry ash powder. This powder was crushed using a mortar-pestle and preheated at 550 °C for 4 h followed by final heating at 1150 °C for 6 h in a muffle furnace, then slowly cooled to room temperature. For dielectric measurements pellets were prepared under pressure of ~4 tons using a hydraulic press and then sintered at 300 °C for 2 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The Sr1-xLaxFe12-yCoyO19 single crystals were grown by the Na2CO3 flux method. Raw materials SrCO3 (99.95 %), Fe2O3 (99.95 %), La2O3 (99.90 %), and Co3O4 (99.95 %) were weighted according to the chemical formula. Na2CO3 (99.95 %) was used as a flux agent with a Na/ Sr molar ratio was 4.995. The mixture was ball-milled and placed in a sealed Pt crucible. Sintering under ambient pressure at 1260 ℃ for 12 h was followed by controlled cooling to 900 ℃ at 2.5 ℃/h to facilitate crystal growth. To separate the single crystals from the melt, the Pt crucible was immersed in a hot dilute HCl solution. The obtained single crystals exhibited a regular hexagonal shape, with sizes reaching up to 5 mm and a thickness of 2–3 mm. For consistency in measurements and to mitigate shape anisotropy, the crystals were uniformly cut into 3×3×1 mm3 rectangles. Polycrystalline powders with nominal compositions of La-Co substitution (x=y=0.1, 0.2, 0.3) were prepared via the conventional solid-state method. SrCO3, Fe2O3, La2O3, and Co3O4 were mixed in a ball mill for 12 h and sintered at 1250 °C for 1 h to obtain these samples.

Synthesis_Procedure: In the present study, raw materials of high purity (≥99.9 %) were utilized to synthesize BaM nanoparticles. Barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2), iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O), and ACV (C2H4O2) were employed as metallic cation sources and natural additive agent, respectively. Additionally, citric acid (C6H8O7⋅H2O) was used as a chelating/combustion agent. All the raw materials were purchased from Merck Chemical Company, and ACV was obtained from an Iranian vinegar producer. Barium hexaferrite nanoparticles were synthesized using the sol–gel auto-combustion method. The influence of different volumes of ACV (0, 5, 10, 15, and 20 ml) on the properties of BaM was investigated, and the samples were denoted as A0, A5, A10, A15, and A20, respectively. The synthesis process involved six main steps, as illustrated in Fig. 1, with varying concentrations of ACV. Initially, non-stoichiometric ratio of Fe and Ba nitrate salts, along with different concentrations ACV, were dissolved in a citric acid solution. Due to the differing solubility rates of Fe and Ba, the thermal stability of hematite (Fe2O3), and Ba evaporation during the process [58], the formation of the hematite phase was inevitable. Therefore, to prevent hematite formation, the molar ratio was adjusted to 10:1 (iron to barium), and the molar ratio of nitrate salts to citric acid was maintained at 1:1.5. Subsequently, ammonia was added dropwise to adjust the pH of the homogenized solution to 9. The sol was then heated at 80 °C for 3 h under constant stirring to produce a seaweed viscous gel. The wet gel was heated at 80 °C for 48 h in an oven. The dried gel was then subjected to a combustion process, resulting in the formation of flaky brown powders as the temperature reached 300 °C. Notably, to crystallize the structure, the nanoparticle precursors were calcined at 800 °C for 4 h in electric furnaces under an air atmosphere.

Then, all solutions were mixed and adjusted the pH to ~9 by gradually adding ammonia. The obtained green solution was stirred for 2 h at ~80 °C to obtain a viscose gel. In the following, to prevent the evaporation of barium and the formation of intermediate phases, the wet viscose gel was immediately transferred into an oven at 80 °C and kept for 48 h. After this step, the dried gel was transferred to an electrical furnace with a temperature of 300 °C, so the auto-combustion process occurred, and the powder containing the precursors was formed. Finally, the prepared precursor was calcined for 4 h at 800 °C to carry out the required reactions to produce the final product. Synthesis_Procedure: Co-Zr substituted SrM (SrCoxZrxFe12-2xO19; 0.00 ≤ x ≤ 0.50) nanoparticles were prepared by employing sol-gel auto-combustion process. The precursors Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3.9H2O, ZrO(NO3)2.H2O, and Co (NO3)2.6H2O were dissolved in deionized (DI) water with an appropriate stoichiometric ratio at constant stirring to form a homogenous solution. Then the uniform solution was mixed with an aqueous citric acid (C6H8O7) mixture and their molar ratio was kept at 1:1. C6H8O7 was selected as a chelating source to inhibit the premature precipitation of metal nitrates during vaporization of H2O content [27,32]. The homogenous mixture was neutralized and maintained at pH 7 by adding NH4OH dropwise with continuous stirring at 100 °C. The solution was kept at constant heating and stirring for 5–6 h that forms a 3D network of metal nitrates changing the initially developed sol into a dark viscous brown gel. Moreover, upon further heating of gel results into spontaneously self-ignition with glowing sparks generating grey flakes with complete evaporation of solvent. Subsequently, the flakes were ground using mortar and pestle and then calcined at 950 °C for 4 h in a temperature-programmed muffle furnace. This process turned the flakes into pure hexagonal phase and eliminated organic solvents from the synthesized compositions. The schematic diagram and real time synthesis process are shown in Figs. 1 and 2, respectively.

The gel was kept inside the oven at 200 °C for 45 min, leading to the formation of a ferrite tree. The ferrite tree was ground using a mortar and pestle, resulting in the formation of nanoparticles. Synthesis_Procedure: Fabrication of five different concentrations of bismuth-doped barium M-type hexagonal ferrite with the structural formula Ba1-XBiXFe12O19(X = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4) was synthesized via the citrate precursor method. Fig. 1 illustrates the step-by-step process for synthesizing Ba1XBiXFe12O19ferrite nanoparticles. To prepare the pure and bismuthdoped barium M-type hexaferrite (where, X = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4), the citrate precursor methodology was used, with raw substances such as Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3, Bi(NO3)3, and citric acid. The chemicals were taken in stoichiometric amounts according to their weight. After that, each of these chemicals was dispersed in 50 mL of distilled water individually with vigorous agitation, and bismuth nitrate was prepared in distilled water containing nitric acid at a 12:1:0.1 M ratio. One after the other, the concentrations of iron and bismuth were incorporated into the barium mixture. In this reaction, citric acid was used as the chelating agent. Afterwards, ammonia hydroxide was added dropwise to stabilize the pH level at 7. The prepared mixture was then heated on a hot plate while agitated for 6 h at 75 degrees Celsius. A viscous wet gel has been formed. The stirring has ended at this moment. The finished product was obtained as a dark powder after the wet gel was continuously heated. With the help of high-temperature furnaces, the obtained powders have been calcined at 850° c for 2 h. Thereafter, Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) was mixed with powder as a binder for making the round shape pellets and followed by heating at 1000° c for 3 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Two sets of Al-substituted barium hexaferrite (BaFe10Al2O19) powders were synthesized by two of most used methods for obtaining magnetic nanoparticles—citric acid auto-combustion and co-precipitation. The corresponding metal nitrates were used as starting materials. A citric acid solution was slowly added to the mixed solution of nitrates as a chelator to form stable complexes with the metal cations. The pH of the solution was reached to 7 by adding ammonium hydroxide and after the homogenization process the solution was slowly evaporated to form a gel. This gel was dehydrated at 120 °C to obtain the barium–iron–alumina citrate precursor. During the dehydration process, the gel turned into a fluffy mass and was burnt in a self-propagating combustion manner. The auto-combusted powders were annealed at 900 °C in air for 7 h. We employed a modified co-precipitation method by applying an ultrasound irradiation during the co-precipitation process. The sonochemical method is advantageous as it is nonhazardous, rapid in reaction rate, and produces very small particles. Ultrasound irradiation causes acoustic cavitation—the formation, growth and implosive collapse of the bubbles in a liquid. The implosive collapse of the bubbles generates localized hot spots of extremely high temperature (∼5000 K) and pressure (∼20 MPa) [18–20]. The corresponding metal nitrates were dissolved in deionized water and the co-precipitation process of metal cations was initiated by adding NaOH at pH = 11. The ratio of Ba:Fe was 1:10 due to the higher solubility of Ba(OH)2 . The high-power ultrasound (750 W) was applied for 15 min to assist the co-precipitation process. The precursors produced were annealed at 900 °C in air for 7 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Using the sol-gel auto combustion method, the desired powdered form of M-type barium hexaferrite having the composition Ba1-xCoxMgxFe12-xO19 (x = 0.4) has been synthesized. For the synthesis, AR grade Ba(NO3)2 (LOBA Chemie., 99% purity), Co(NO3)2 .6H2O (LOBA Chemie., 99% purity), Mg(NO3)2 .6H2O (LOBA Chemie., 99% purity), Fe(NO3)3.9H2O (LOBA Chemie., 98% purity) and citric acid (LOBA Chemie., 99.5% purity) are used. The nitrate salts are initially taken in stoichiometric ratios and an aqueous solution is prepared by mixing and dissolving in distilled water. A magnetic stirrer accompanies the mixing procedure. The usage of a magnetic stirrer helps to prepare a less contaminated sample and is easy to properly mix the solution as well. Citric acid is mixed with the salt solution in a ratio of 1:1.5. This makes the whole solution acidic. For the formation of barium hexaferrite, the pH should be neutral. Drop by drop addition of ammonium hydroxide results in the lowering of pH value. The solution thus has a pH value of approximately 6.7. The whole solution is then simultaneously heated and magnetically stirred for 4-6 hours under a temperature range of 80 – 85 degrees Celsius. The following reaction occurs. (1 − x)Ba(NO3)2 + xMg(NO3)3 + xCo(NO3)2 + (12 − x)Fe(NO3)3·9H2O —(NH4OH, Heat)→ Ba1−xCoxMgxFe12−xO19. Evaporation occurs and the solution converts to a brown viscous gel. Upon further heating of the gel, the auto combustion reaction takes place. Synthesis_Procedure: The raw materials of ≥ 98 percent purity was used to produce the undoped and copper-doped BaFe12O19 nanohexaferrites. These raw materials includes copper nitrate (Cu(NO3)2⋅3H2O, SimSon), ferric nitrate (Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, SimSon), barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)3⋅9H2O, Merck), citric acid (C6H8O7, SimSon), ethylene glycol (C2H6O2, SimSon), and ammonia solution (NH4OH, SimSon). Here, the citric acid is used as a fuel, ethylene glycol as a gel precursor, and ammonia solution to maintain the required solution’s pH. The stoichiometric amounts of all these reagents used for the production of undoped and copper-doped BaFe12O19 nanohexaferrites are provided in Table 1. Metals inorganic sol–gel auto-combustion approach was used to generate the BaFe12O19 nanohexaferrites, Ba1-0.5xCu0.5xFe12O19, (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3). First, two separate solutions of metal nitrates and citric acid with stoichiometric concentrations were made in 50 ml of distilled water. These solutions were then stirred on a magnetic stirrer with a hot plate (30 °C). The solutions were stirred until the starting materials were completely dissolved, or until the stirring stopped. Then, add the metal nitrates solution to the necessary solution of citric acid and stir it at 40 °C. After that, ammonia solution was added to the solution, and it was stirred at a temperature of 60 °C in order to maintain a pH level of 7. Then, the ethylene glycol precursor was added to the neutral solution to make the gel quickly. Lastly, ash material was made by heating the gel at 100 °C. The ash material was first crushed into finer particles using a mortar pestle, and then it was calcinated in a muffle furnace at a temperature of 1100 °C (5 h). After being calcinated, the material was then in a state to investigate its structural and magnetic traits. The scheme for producing nanohexaferrites by the sol–gel autocombustion method is shown in Fig. 2.

Synthesis_Procedure: SGACT has been used to synthesize Ca2+-doped BaM. The chemicals used such as calcium nitrate, ferric nitrate, barium nitrate and citric acid (AR grade, ≥99 % purity), have been obtained from LOBA Chemie and are utilized as such, without any further purification. The salts of metal nitrates were dissolved in double distilled water in desired proportion (Table 1). Afterward, a magnetic stirrer was used for mixing the citric acid. A 25 % solution of ammonia has been added drop by drop in order to keep the pH at 7.0. The hot plate was used to raise the temperature of the resultant solution to 90–100 °C. By constant heating, the excess amount of water evaporates after a few hours and then, a gel with brown color like honey was produced. The brown gel has been kept in a hot oven maintained at a temperature between 200 and 250 °C for 1 h so that, auto-combustion takes place. After completion of the autocombustion reaction, the precursor material of mixed metal oxide was formed. A mortar pestle was used to grind the precursor material until it is converted to a fine powder. Impurities were removed from this ground powder by calcinating it 900 °C for 6 h with the help of a muffle furnace and changing the amorphous phase into crystalline. Lastly, the calcinated powder was further sintered at 950 °C for 6 h in a muffle furnace and then it was pressed into pellets using 2 % of polyvinyl alcohol solution (PVA) in a hydraulic press to report its dielectric traits.

After that, the calcined samples were grinded into a fine powdered form using mortar and pestle so as to perform the further characterizations.

Synthesis_Procedure: Hexagonal Sr0.7La0.3Fe11.75-xAlxCo0.25O19 (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.12) samples were prepared by the conventional ceramic process. The starting materials were SrCO3 (99% purity), La2O3 (99.9% purity), Fe2O3 (98% purity), Co2O3 (99.99% purity) and Al2O3 (99.0% purity). The raw materials were mixed together in the chemical composition of Sr0.7La0.3Fe11.75-xAlxCo0.25O19 (x = 0, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12). Mixtures of raw materials were milled in water by planetary ball milling for 3 h with an angular velocity of 300 rpm, the process obeys the condition of ballpower ratio of 12:1. After that, dry the mixed powders in an oven at 120 °C. Then, the powders were sintered in a muffle furnace at 1250 °C for 3 h in air and M-type hexaferrites can be obtained. The obtained powders were grounded using a vibration mill to obtain fine powder, which is convenient for further measurement. In addition, some powder of the sample x = 0.08 was further ball-milled to 1 μm, then pressed into shape under magnetic field with the same direction as that of pressing. The molded blank was sintered in air at 1230 °C for 2 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The designed (Ni,Cr,Zr)-co-doped BaFe12-3xNixCrxZrxO19 ferrite magnetic powders were synthesized by traditional solid-state reaction using BaCO3 (99%), Fe2O3 (99%), NiO (99%), Cr2O3 (99%) and ZrO2 (99%) as raw powders. Among the raw powders, BaCO3 and Fe2O3 were bought from Macklin Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China), NiO and Cr2O3 were purchased from Xilong Chemical Co. Ltd. (Guangzhou, China), and ZrO2 was bought from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). All the raw powders were used as received. During typical synthesis process, the raw powders were first weighed respectively in the designed stoichiometric ratio, which were then mixed together by grinding for 6 h in a planetary ball mill with ZrO2 balls as the grinding media and ethanol as the dispersion media. After drying at 100 °C for 4 h and grinding in an agate mortar, the resultant powder mixtures were ready for calcination. Based on the results of TG-DSC thermal analysis, the powder mixtures were calcined in a muffle oven at 1075 °C in an air atmosphere for 3 h. Afterwards, the as-calcined powder chunks were crashed and ground by a secondary ball milling as mentioned above for 4 h. After drying at 105 °C for 24 h, grinding and sieving, the proposed, pure-phase (Ni,Cr,Zr)-co-doped BaFe12-3xNixCrxZrxO19 ferrite magnetic powders were finally obtained. During the typical process for preparing ceramics, the as-obtained fine magnetic powders were first pressed by dry pressing into green tablets with a diameter of 6 mm and a thickness of 2 mm at 4 MPa. Afterwards, based on the results of VHTD analysis, the green tablets were sintered at 1350 °C for 3 h by heating up at a rate of 5 °C/min, and the sintering atmosphere is air, finally obtaining pure-phase, full-dense ceramic samples.

The solutions were prepared with the expectation that in the final volume (80 ml) the concentration of iron ions would be 0.25 M, the (Fe3++Co2+)/Ba2+ ratio would be 9, and the OH-/NO3- ratio would be 2.5. Separation of the precipitate formed and the liquid solution was carried out using a centrifuge. Next, the precipitate was dried at 90 °C for 8 h. The dry residue was ground in an agate mortar and annealed in a muffle furnace in air. The heating rate was 15°/min, the final temperature was 900 °C, and the annealing time was 1 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The chemical compositions of Zr4+-Y3+ co-doped Ba-Sr hexaferrite (x=0.00, 0.20, 0.35, 0.50) were prepared using the sol-gel auto-combustion method. Stoichiometric amounts of metal nitrates (Ba(NO3)2, Sr (NO3)2, ZrO(NO3)2.2H2O, Y(NO3)2.6H2O, and Fe(NO3)2.9H2O) were dissolved together in deionized water to obtain a transparent solution. An aqueous solution of citric acid was mixed in metal nitrate solution while keeping the metal nitrate to citrate ratio as 1:1. Citric acid was chosen as a chelating agent to suppress the precipitation of metal nitrates during the evaporation of water contents. The pH of 7 is asserted via dropwise addition of NH4OH solution, followed by continuous stirring at 100 °C. This yields a viscous brown gel that automatically ignites and burns with glowing flints after complete evaporation of water contents, yielding grey flakes. The calcination of these flakes was carried out at 900 °C for 6 hours, followed by grinding using mortar and pestle to obtain Zr-Y substituted hexaferrite nanoparticles.

Synthesis_Procedure: In the present work, a series of aluminium doped BaFe11.4-xAlxCo0.6O19 hexaferrites with different content (x = 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, and 1.6) have prepared via co-precipitation method followed by Sonochemical process. In the first step, stoichiometric quantity of the above mentioned salts are dissolved in distilled water separately by constantly stirring using magnetic stirrer. All of the prepared solutions are also homogenised separately by using Great sonic device. After that all of the prepared solutions are mixed in a single beaker and put on the hot plate. Then the solution is constantly stirring using magnetic stirrer for four hours. The temperature of the solution is maintained 60–70 ˚C during the entire process. The PH of the solution is maintained 11–12 by using NaOH. After being stirrer the solution for 4 h then, it is sonicated for 40 min for better results. Centrifuge machine is used to separate the paste of the sample from water. The paste of the sample is then dried by using oven for 12 h at 100 ˚C temperature. The dried powders were then placed within a ceramic crucible and allowed to calcine for four hours at a temperature of 700 °C. After that, these powder were gradually cooled to room temperature. Synthesis_Procedure: The raw materials used for the experiment consisted of ferric oxide (Fe2O3; 99 %), barium carbonate (BaCO3; 99 %), and samarium trioxide (Sm2O3; 99.99 %). The ferric oxide and barium carbonate were produced by Aladdin (Shanghai, China) and the samarium trioxide was produced by McLean (Shanghai, China), and they were used without any further purification. According to the chemical formula Ba1− xSmxFe12O19 and weighed out accurately according to the respective stoichiometric ratio, the quantities of each of the raw materials are listed in Table 1. To synthesize M-type barium ferrite, a mixture of mill balls (ZrO2, 350 g), mixed raw materials (35 g), and anhydrous ethanol (35 g) with a mass ratio of ~ 10:1:1 was placed into a nylon pot. After wet grinding for 5 h in a ball mill, they were transferred to bellows and dried at 90 °C for 2 h. The mixture was filtered through a sieve to separate the grinding balls and powder, and a sample of 14 g of the separated powder was removed. A tablet press was used to produce a round pellet at a pressure of 15 MPa. The pressed round pellet was placed in a muffle furnace and sintered from room temperature to 1250 °C at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. It was kept at that temperature for 2 h and then cooled to room temperature in the furnace. The resulting calcined particles were crushed and dry-ground to form a powder with a particle size of less than 100 μm before use.

According to the chemical formula Ba1− xSmxFe12O19 and weighed out accurately according to the respective stoichiometric ratio, the quantities of each of the raw materials are listed in Table 1. To synthesize M-type barium ferrite, a mixture of mill balls (ZrO2, 350 g), mixed raw materials (35 g), and anhydrous ethanol (35 g) with a mass ratio of ~ 10:1:1 was placed into a nylon pot. After wet grinding for 5 h in a ball mill, they were transferred to bellows and dried at 90 °C for 2 h. The mixture was filtered through a sieve to separate the grinding balls and powder, and a sample of 14 g of the separated powder was removed. A tablet press was used to produce a round pellet at a pressure of 15 MPa. The pressed round pellet was placed in a muffle furnace and sintered from room temperature to 1250 °C at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. It was kept at that temperature for 2 h and then cooled to room temperature in the furnace. The resulting calcined particles were crushed and dry-ground to form a powder with a particle size of less than 100 μm before use.

Synthesis_Procedure: The materials used for experiments were analytically pure Fe2O3, BaCO3, and Pr6O11, and were all products from Aladdin’s factories (CHN). The raw materials, pure BaCO3, Fe2O3, and Pr6O11 powders, were correctly weighed according to the stoichiometric ratio for the chemical formula Ba1−xPrxFe12O19. The balls and raw materials’ powders were accurately weighed according to the mass ratio of 10:1 and then put into the Pulverisette 5 high-energy ball mill (Flying Germany). A certain proportion of pure deionized water was added as the process control agent. The rotating speed of the ball mill was set to 150 r/min, and the ball-milling time was 8 h. Each ball-milling process for 2 h constitutes one cycle. There were four cycles, and the interval between every two cycles was 15 min. After full ball milling, the resulting material was put into a blast dryer at 90 °C for 6 h. The ball-milled material was separated, and the obtained 14-g powder was pressed into a round cake using a tablet press under 15-MPa pressure and was sintered in the muffle furnace. The heating rate was 5 °C/min, rising from room temperature to 1200 °C. This temperature was maintained for 2 h, and then the furnace was cooled to room temperature.

Synthesis_Procedure: The following chemicals received from Merck with high purity were used for the synthesis of Sr0.8Ni0.2Fe12−2xMoxO19 (x ≤ 0.35) NHFs by sol–gel auto-combustion. Firstly, the stoichiometric amount of Sr(NO3)2, Ni(NO3)2.6H2O, and Fe(NO3)3.9H2O was dissolved in 50-ml DI H2O at 80 °C. The specific amount of MoO3 was thawed in 10-ml concentrated HCl under vigorous stirring at 150 °C. Afterward, both the metal nitrate and the MoO3 solution were mixed with adding 13 g of citric acid (C6H8O7) under stirring at 80 °C. The mixture solution’s pH was adjusted to 7 by ammonium solution, and then set the temperature at 150 °C for 35 min followed by heating at 330 °C for 2 h. The solution was vaporized, and then turned into gel and finally burned and turned to powder with releasing gases. The resultant powder was calcined at 1100 °C for 5 h to get the Sr0.8Ni0.2Fe12−2xMoxO19 (x ≤ 0.35) NHFs. The weight of used each precursor corresponding to each ‘x’ is given Table 1.

Synthesis_Procedure: Iron oxide (Fe2O3; 99%), barium carbonate (BaCO3; 99%), praseodymium oxide (Pr6O11; 99.99%), and Al oxide (Al2O3; 99%) were used as starting materials without any treatment. All raw materials are products produced by Aladdin’s factories. Table 1 shows the specific mass of pure BaCO3, Fe2O3, Pr6O11, and Al2O3 powders required based on different Al doping amounts according to the chemical formula Ba0.85Pr0.15Fe12-xAlxO19 (x = 0.0–1.0). M-type ferrite was synthesized by a solid-phase reaction. Put the weighed raw materials according to the chemical formula Ba0.85Pr0.15Fe12-xAlxO19 (x = 0.0–1.0) into a PULVERISETTE 5 high-energy ball mill (German Feichi) for ball milling and mixing. The mass ratio of the grinding ball and powder raw material was 10:1, adding the same quality of absolute ethanol as the raw material as the process control agent, the speed of the ball mill was set to 150 rpm, and the ball mill time was 8 h. To prevent the excessive temperature in the process of ball mill caused by extra reaction, 2-h interval of each ball mill was set at 15 min. After the material is mixed through full ball milling, it is dried in the air drying oven at 90 °C for 4 h, the ball material is separated, and the 14-g powder is pressed into a round cake shape with a diameter of 30 mm and a thickness of 15 mm under the pressure of 15 mpa by a sheet press. Then, the powder was sintered in a Muffle furnace at 1250 °C for 2 h. The heating rate of the Muffle furnace was 5 °C/min, and the pellets were cooled at room temperature. Finally, the calcined pellets were pulverized, and some samples were dried to a particle size less than 100 µm.

Synthesis_Procedure: All of the samples of M-type hexaferrite Ba0.8In0.2Fe12−xNixO19 (x = 0.00, 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00) used in this investigation were made using the conventional solid-state reaction method. The starting materials BaCO3, Al2O3, In2O3, and Fe2O3, purchased from Aladdin chemicals and contained a purity level of 99.9% were mixed according to the stoichiometric ratios by using a planetary ball mill, and the sample was ground for 10 h while the components were combined with zirconia balls and ethanol as a medium in nylon jars. To remove any remaining moisture before further processing, the material was removed from the ball mill, dried, and ground. To remove the carbonates, the material was calcined at 1100 °C. After that, it was exposed to a 6-h ball milling process before being dried and powdered once more. Using a vibration mill, the material was further broken down into particles smaller than 90 nm. The material was then sintered for 2 h at a temperature of 1250 °C. The resultant solid solution was pressed into pellets of 12 mm diameter and 1.2 mm thickness for scanning electron microscopy investigation. The pellets underwent another sintering procedure at 900 °C to remove any PVA binder leftover. The generalized chemical equation for the reaction can be as: BaCO3 + In2O3 + Fe2O3 + NiO + O2 → Ba0.8In0.2Fe12−xNixO19 where x is the amount of Nickel oxide added and can be varied depending on the requirement of the desired material.

Synthesis_Procedure: The La-Co-co-substituted Sr M-type hexaferrites with the nominal compositions of Sr1−xLaxFe12−xCoxO19, (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.4) were prepared via a solid-state reaction in air. Also, ballmilled powders were mixed with a distilled water and pelletized with the uniaxial press at 1.5 tons, while applying the external magnetic field of 15 kOe to produce c-axis-aligned samples (MFP samples). We also prepared uniaxially pressed samples (1 inch diameter) at a pressure of 220 MPa and followed by CIP (cold isostatic pressing) with 1.5 tons of non-MFP2 samples. The resulting pellets were sintered at 1230 °C for 2 h, in air.

Synthesis_Procedure: The pure phase BaFe12-xGdxO19 with (x = 0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0) was prepared using chemical based citrate precursor sol–gel method. Chemicals used were of high purity grade namely, Ba(NO3)2, Gd(NO3)3, Fe(NO3)3 (Alfa Aesar, 99.9% purity). Citric acid was used as fuel for self-igniting reaction. We first dissolve stoichiometric amount of reactant nitrates into minimal amount of deionized water. Then these individual solutions are poured into beaker containing citric acid solution. We keep this solution on a hot plate stirrer and add ammonia drop wise to shift its pH to 7. Thereafter this solution is left for continuous stirring with temperature set at 120 ℃ till a gel like substance is obtained. Then this jelly substance is kept inside hot air oven set at 220 ℃ for 30 min, resulting into a voluminous like ash powder which is grinded to fine powders with Mortar and Pestle. Synthesis_Procedure: The polycrystalline BaM ferrites doped with La3+, with chemical formula Ba1-xLaxFe12O19-δ, where δ = x/2 is the non-compensated oxygen and x = 0.0, 0.1 and 0.6, were prepared by the conventional solid-state reaction method It by using high purity Fe2O3, La2O3 and BaCO3 from Sigma-Aldrich-Brazil. The specific chemical formula was: BaFe12O19 (named as BML00) for pure barium hexaferrite, Ba0.9La0.1Fe12O19-δ (named as BML01) for x = 0.1 and Ba0.4La0.6Fe12O19-δ (named as BML06) for x = 0.6. The x values were selected by the criterion of the La3+ cation solubility limit: for x = 0.1 (there is total solubility) and for x = 0.6 the La3+ cation quantity is above the solubility limit within the BaM structure [20]. The precursor’s oxides were mixed in the desired stoichiometry and milled for 8 h to obtain finer particles, then were calcined at 1000°C for 8 h with a heating rate of 20°C/min. The calcined powders were milled for 4 h and immediately sieved. After this, the powders were pressed at 2.6 Ton/cm2 in 10 mm diameter disc-shaped samples and sintered at 1200°C for 45 min, with a heating rate of 10°C/min.

Synthesis_Procedure: Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, Al(NO3)3⋅9H2O, and glycine were all purchased from Aladdin and used without further purification. The porous BaFe12− xAlxO19 nanomaterials were prepared by a sol-gel auto-combustion method followed by annealing treatment in air atmosphere. Nitrate salts and glycine were used as the precursor and fuel, respectively. According to the composition of BaFe12− xAlxO19, stoichiometric amount precursors of Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O, Al(NO3)3⋅9H2O were dissolved in 50 ml of deionized water under magnetic stirring. Glycine was dissolved into the nitrate solution to give a molar ratio of total metal ions to glycine of 1:2. The pH value of the above solution was adjusted to 7 by adding the ammonium hydroxide dropwise and magnetically stirred for 30 min before heating it on a hotplate at 200 °C. After the evaporation of water, the resulting thick sol burned spontaneously to give a raw oxide powder. The raw powders without Al3+ substitution was annealed at 800, 1000, 1200, 1400 and 1600 °C for 4 h, respectively to optimize the annealing temperature. Then the raw powders with various Al3+ contents were annealed at the optimized annealing temperature for 4 h to obtain the BaFe12− xAlxO19 nanomaterials.

Synthesis_Procedure: Pure BaFe12O19 and BaFe11Ti0.5M0.5O19 (M = Co2+, Ni2+, Zn2+) hexaferrites were prepared via co-precipitation method. The precursors used for the synthesis were Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3.9H2O, Co(NO3)2.6H2O, Ni(NO3)2.6H2O, Zn(NO3)2.6H2O and TiCl4. The pH of the solution was controlled by using KOH as a catalyst. Firstly, 100 ml of distilled water was used to dissolve the stoichiometric amounts of nitrates. The dissolved nitrates were added dropwise in KOH solution and were left for stirring at 70 °C. The precipitates were formed after 2 h of stirring on the hotplate. The obtained precipitates were washed several times with deionized water and then dried overnight in an oven at 100 °C. The obtained powders were ground and annealed at 1000 °C for 12 h. Finally, annealed powders were compressed in the form of pellets at a pressure of 5 tons/cm2 using a hydraulic press and then sintered at 1200 °C for 6 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Ca2+ doped, barium M-type hexaferrite (BaCaM, Ba1-xCaxFe12O19) was synthesized with a 1:1 ratio of metal nitrate to fuel (citric acid) by sol-gel auto-combustion method. The nitrate salts of barium, calcium and iron were dissolved separately in desired stoichiometric ratio in distilled water and then citric acid (fuel, reducing agent, chelating agent) was added at ambient temperature. In order to maintain solution pH to 7, dilute solution of ammonia was added with burette dropwise. The resultant solution was heated for 6–8 h on hot plate at 80–100 °C. Excessive water evaporates with continuous heating and dark brownish gel has been produced. This dark brownish gel like honey was placed in the hot air oven for auto combustion at 200–250 °C for 1 h. Auto combustion process converts the highly viscous gel into fluffy and highly porous burned paper like grayish black ash precursor. The ash precursor with mortar pastel was crushed into fine powder and then calcined at different temperature (900–1300 °C) in the muffle furnace for 6 h using temperature gradient of 100 °C/h. During calcination process the residual (carbon & nitrates based) impurities and secondary phases were eliminated and pure BaCaM phase formed. The solution (of 2% polyvinyl alcohol binder) was properly mixed with BaCaM powder. PVA and BaCaM powder mixture dried, ground and sieved powder properly. This dried powder was pressed (using 5 metric ton pressure for 60 s) into 10 mm pellets. To remove the PVA residue, these pellets were sintered (for 2 h at 1000 °C).

Synthesis_Procedure: The compositions Sr0.5Ba0.5Fe12O19 and Sr0.5Ba0.5RE0.6Fe11.4O19, [RE = La, Yb, Sm, Gd, Er, Eu, Dy] have been prepared by the sol-gel method, using the initial extra pure 99.9% materials of (SrCl2.6H2O), (Fe(NO3)3.9H2O), (BaCo3) together with the rare earth oxides (La2O3, Yb2O3, Sm2O3, Gd2O3, Er2O3, Eu2O3, and Dy2O3). The citric acid (C6H8O7) was used as an organic fuel and pure ammonia solution (NH4OH) for adjusting the pH value at 7. Stoichiometric amounts of the chloride, nitrate, and carbonate materials of Sr2+, Fe3+, and Ba2+, respectively, were dissolved in deionized water and stirred for 20 min. Besides, the required weights of rare earth oxides are dissolved separately in 10 ml conc. HCl and stirred for 45 min. The clearness of the RE3+ oxide solution is an indication that the oxides are completely dissolved. The solutions of the metals; Sr2+, Fe3+, Ba3+, and RE3+ were mixed with citric acid in a molar ratio (1:1). The type of fuel plays an important role in determining the intensity of auto-combustion reaction and the time required for thermal treatment. The ratio of the metals solutions to the fuel can affect the magnetic parameters and the grain size [6,13]. Ammonia solution (NH4OH) was added to the mixture to obtain a solution with (pH = 7). The nanoparticles prepared at lower values of pH, have high agglomerations compared to that prepared at (pH = 7), while the combustion rate is significantly affected by the pH value in the mixed solution. The combustion rate is enhanced by increasing the pH value from 2.5 to 7 [6]. The obtained mixture heated and stirred at 80 °C and 350 °C for getting a viscous gel. Subsequently, and under the same temperature, the gel burnt and converted to brown powder. Finally, the obtained powders of the initial hexaferrite samples; Sr0.5Ba0.5Fe12O19 and Sr0.5Ba0.5RE0.6Fe11.4O19, [RE = La, Yb, Sm, Gd, Er, Eu, Dy] were calcinated at 1100 °C for 30 h to eliminate the residuals of organic materials. The powder was finally sintered at 1200 °C for 10 h to exclude the chance of secondary phase formation.

Synthesis_Procedure: Polycrystalline samples of Sr1− x LaxFe12O19 (x = 0.1, 0.3, and 0.6), were prepared by the conventional solid state reaction method. Powders of SrCO3 (98% purity), La2O3 (98% purity) and Fe2O3 (98% purity) were mixed at the desired stoichiometric ratios according to the following chemical equation: (1 − x)SrCO3 + (x/2)La2O3 + 6Fe2O3 ⟶ Sr(1−x)LaxFe12O(19+x/2) + CO2. (1) The mixed powders were milled and calcined in air at 1000 °C for 8 h. These samples will be hereafter referred to as SCL01 (x = 0.1), SCL03 (x = 0.3), and SCL06 (x = 0.6), respectively. At last, the calcined powder were directly sintered in a SPS 1050 Dr. Sinter apparatus manufactured by Sumitomo Coal Mining Co. Ltd., Japan. The powder, for each La-content, were placed inside a cylindrical graphite die with dimensions of 50 mm (outer diameter) and 20 mm (inner diameter) and between two graphite plungers of ∼ 40 mm in height. In order to protect the die and facilitate the sample release after consolidation, graphite foils were inserted between the internal surfaces of the die and between the top and the bottom surfaces of the sample and the graphite plungers. The die was then placed inside the chamber of the SPS apparatus and sintering was formed under vacuum (from 10 to ∼ 30 Pa). The consolidation temperature, TD , the consolidation time, tD , and the heating rate, TD /tr , for all samples were 900 °C, 5 min, and ∼ 175 °C/min, respectively. The temperature was measured during the consolidation process by using a (K-type) thermocouple, which was inserted into a small hole in one side of the graphite die. After the sintering process, each sample was first allowed to naturally cool for about 50 min and then removed from the die. The maximum uniaxial compacting pressure used to consolidate all samples was 50 MPa, reached by a gradual increase during the first three minutes. All the above experimental conditions are similar to that reported elsewhere for the pure SrFe12O19 samples [34–36]. The obtained sample be hereafter referred to as SPL01 (x = 0.1), SPL03 (x = 0.3), and SPL06 (x = 0.6), respectively.

After the precursors have been well mixed in the same temperature (80c) for about 2 h, we increase the temperature is raised to 180C, and a thick gel form. The result was a swollen black powder. To remove any organic product or unreacted glycine, the powders were heat-treated in a hot air oven at 700C for 2 h. then the powders were pressed into thin pellets with a diameter of 8 mm and a thickness of 1 mm, and sintered at various temperatures: (i) 900C for 30 min; (ii) 1000C for 30 min; (iii) 1100C for 2 h. The AR grade chemicals of BaCl2.2H2O, NiCl2.6H2O, ZnCl2, and FeCl3 were used as precursors. Further, the stoichiometric amount of these salts was dissolved in deionized water. Afterward, the NaOH pellets were added to the resultant solution to get the pH = 12. Further, the aqueous solution was poured into a 300 mL of Teflon lined stainless steel autoclave and it was kept in a hot air oven. The reaction was carried out at 160 °C for 10 h. The final product was washed repeatedly using deionized water and ethanol until the pH = 7 was attained. Then it was dried at 80 °C in the oven. Synthesis_Procedure: All samples were prepared using the standard ceramic process by the planetary mill (Pulverisette; Fritsch GmbH, Germany). The raw materials used in this paper were BaCo3 (99% purity, Aladdin), Y2O3 (99% purity, Aladdin), Fe2O3 (98% purity), and Co2O3 (99% purity, Aladdin). The raw materials were mixed in the planetary mill using two sizes of hardened steel balls with diameters of 5 and 8 mm, obeying the ratio of 2:1, and milled in water for 3 h with an angular velocity of 200 rpm according to the ball-to-powder weight ratio of 15:1. Then, the mixture were dried at 100 °C in an oven when the milling process is over. And then, as-prepared sample were sintered in a muffle furnace at 1250 °C for 3 h. Finally, the mixture powder is cooled down to room temperature and crushed to particles by a vibration mill.

Synthesis_Procedure: WOWS sol–gel approach is employed to create cobalt-samariam (Co-Sm) doped M-type barium hexaferrite nanocrystalline materials of various compositions (Z = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6). The synthesized materials are listed in Table II. Compared to conventional methods this approach route allows a number of significant advantage that make the technique promising for the construction of materials tailored to specific application.27–29 This approach is highly feasible, cost-effective and efficient, and precise control over the doping level is also easier in this process. The starting materials taken for synthesis are summarized in Table III. The hexaferrite samples of different compositions were synthesized by using stoichiometric amounts of Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Sm(NO3)3·6H2O and Co(NO3)2·6H2O. To obtain a solution, the metal salts were dissolved in freshly distilled 1,2-ethanediol. To dissolve the metal salts homogeneously in 1,2-ethanediol, the molar ratio of the metal salts to 1,2-ethanediol was maintained at 1:13. At room temperature, the mixture of metal salts in 1,2-ethanediol was vigorously stirred for 30 min to afford homogeneous solution, then the temperature of system was linearly increased to nearly 200°C with continuous and vigorous stirring until a thick metal nitrates gel was produced (Scheme 1). Next, temperature of the metal nitrates gel was increased to about 350°C under continuous and vigorous stirring, which led to drying out of the metal nitrates gel. The process generates a soft compound via a redox reaction in which the nitrates ions of metal salts behave as the oxidiser and 1,2-ethanediol behaves as the reducer. Under the same experimental conditions, this procedure was repeated for the preparation of each product. In the next step, the product was crushed with the assistance of pestle and mortar to fine powder (Scheme 1). Then, to increase crystallinity, the product was calcined at 1200°C for 2 h in a silicon carbide furnace in air. The obtained fine powder was then pelletized to disks 13.0 mm in diameter and 4.0 mm in thickness through applying a uniaxial load of about 1000 psi for 15 min. The pellets were sintered at 550°C for 20 min.

Synthesis_Procedure: Samples of BaFe12−2xCoxO19 (BHFC) having compositions (x = 0.0, 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2) were prepared via a chemical method. Analytical grade chemicals were used for this synthesis. Barium nitrate Ba(NO3)2 (99% Merck, India), iron nitrate Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (98% Merck, India) and Co(NO3)2·6H2O (97% Merck, India) were taken as starting materials at their stoichiometric ratios. The metal nitrates of Ba, Fe and Co mentioned above were dissolved in doubled-distilled water, and then a calculated amount of citric acid (C6H8O7·H2O, 99% Merck, India) acting as a complexing agent as per equivalent to metal ions was also added for chelation of Ba+2, Fe+3 and Co+2 ions. The resulting solution was dried on a hot plate/magnetic stirrer at 70–80°C to obtain BHFC powder, after removal of water, which was burnt with the sooty flame. The synthesized resulting powder was ground and calcined at 800°C for 8 h, and then used to make cylindrical pellets of 11.5 mm × 1.00 mm by using polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as a binder and applying pressure of 5 tons with a hydraulic press. Finally, the pellets were sintered at 1150°C for 12 h in an electrical furnace at a scanning rate of 4°C/min.

Synthesis_Procedure: A set of hexagonal ferrites Ba1-xSrxFe12O19 with strontium concentration 0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.75 were synthesized by the sol–gel method. The initial components with the purity of ≥99.9 % BaCo3, SrCl2.6H2O, and Fe(NO3)3 were stoichiometrically mixed with adding to citric acid C6H8O7 in 1:1 molar ratio. Thereafter, the distilled water was added to the mixture forming a solution with pH adjusted to be 7 using the ammonia solution. The obtained mixture heated and stirred at 80 oC and 350 oC in a muffle furnace for getting a viscous gel. Subsequently, and under the same temperature, the gel burnt and converted to brown powder. Synthesis_Procedure: The chemical composition of multi substituted barium hexaferrite (BaCoxCuxZr2xFe12−4xO4 where x=0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5) were synthesized via sol–gel autocombustion route. Substituted barium hexagonal ferrite was prepared by taking high purity barium chloride dehydrate (BaCl2.2H2O, 99.99%, Merck), iron (III) chloride (FeCl3, 98%, Merck), zirconium (IV) oxynitrate hydrate (ZrO(NO3)2.xH2O, 99%, SigmaAldrich), copper (II) chloride dehydrate (CuCl2.2H2O, 99%, Merck), cobalt chloride hexahydrate (CoCl2.6H2O, 99-102%, Merck) and polyvinyl alcohol [CH2CH(OH)]n as the starting materials. Finally, nonstoichiometric amounts of BaCl2. 2H2O, FeCl3, CuCl2.2H2O, CoCl2.6H2O, ZrO(NO3)2.xH2O and citric acid were mixed in an specific amount of deionized water with 2 wt.% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) used as surfactant. The sol solution was heated under constant stirring at 70 °C about 1 h to form a homogenous solution. Ammonia solution (1.5 M) was added slowly to the solution until the pH value of the solution was adjusted to 7. To obtain a viscous gel, the pH value of the system sustained during the water evaporation process at 90 °C. Also, the viscous dark gel was heated with low heating rate for about 12 h at 180 °C until the gel combusted and obtained a primary powder. Then, dried fluffy precursors were annealed at 900 °C for 3 h. All samples were subjected under the same condition to have a meaningful comparison between their results in the air atmosphere to form hexagonal phase.

Above mention nitrates are utilized correspond to their stoichiometric amount to prepare a solution in deionized water. The stock solution is placed on magnetic stirrer and to get homogeneous solution continuous heat and stirring is employed. The 1:1.5 is the molar ratio of citric acid utilized to mixed metals. Then ammonia solution is further added drop wise by using burette and stirring was continued to sustain the pH at 7-8 level. Stop dropping ammonia and solution was stirrer and heated in between 70-80οC until water evaporated. When gel formation was started we gave 200οC temperature until we acquired fluffy powder. Then powder was grinded by using agate mortar and pestle. After grinding we placed this powder in an electrical furnace to dry it completely at 300οC for half hour after it powder should be furnace cooled. Then we again grind that powder and placed in electric furnace for 8 hours at 950οC. After completing all procedure we got brownish black powder.

Synthesis_Procedure: In the present work, analytical grade BaCO3, Fe2O3 and TiO2 of 99.9% purity from Sigma-Aldrich were used to prepare BaFe12-xTixO19, (x = 0.0, 0.5) by three-step calcination method. Precursors were weighed in stoichiometric composition and wet-mixed for 3 h using planetary ball mill. As mixed powders were subsequently pelletized at a pressure of 150 MPa using hydraulic press. In the first step, as-prepared pellets were calcined at 1200 °C for 3 h using muffle furnace. Heating and cooling rate were kept constant at 5 °C/min. The calcined pellets were pulverized to powder using vibratory mill. In the second step, pulverized powder was pelletized and re-calcined at 1200 °C for 3 h. Similar step was repeated for third step calcination. The pure BaM powder obtained from first, second and third step calcination process were labelled as BaM 1, BaM 2 and BaM 3, whereas Ti-substituted powders as BaTiM 1, BaTiM 2 and BaTiM 3 respectively. As-calcined powders from each step were mixed with binder (5% PVA) and pressed in rectangular die (16 × 8 mm) at a pressure of 250 MPa. Thickness of pellets were kept constant to 4 mm. The as-pressed pellets were sintered at 1250 °C for 1 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The method used for the preparation of the hexaferrites is solution combustion synthesis. Solution combustion synthesis (SCS) is a versatile, simple, and rapid process, which allows the active synthesis of a variety of nano-size materials. This process involves a self-stimulated reaction in a homogeneous solution of different oxidizers (metal nitrates) and fuels (citric acid, sucrose). Depending on the type of the precursors and the process conditions, the SCS may occur as either volume or layer-by-layer propagating combustion modes. The strontium hexaferrite, barium hexaferrite, and calcium hexaferrite powders are prepared using solution combustion synthesis. The Al and Ce substituted SrFe12O19 particles were prepared via solution combustion method using nitrate salts. According to the composition Sr0.9Ce0.1Fe10Al2O19 stoichiometric amounts of Sr(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Al(NO3)3·9H2O, Ce(NO3)3·6H2O were dissolved in deionized water. The fuels include Sucrose (C12H22O11) and Citric acid (C6H8O7). The solution is then hot stirred at a temperature of 80 °C for few hours until a brown viscous gel was formed. In this process a mixed fuel of sucrose and citric acid was used for the process of combustion. Then the solutions were allowed to cool to room temperatures by then NaOH was then added as buffer solution. The produced gel was ignited by keeping the furnace at a temperature of 300 °C producing large amounts of gas, resulting in the formation of lightweight voluminous powder. The calcinations has done at three different temperatures, namely 800 °C, 900 °C, 1100 °C in the furnace for about 12 h. The resultant powder is characterized further for required structural, microstructural and magnetic properties.

Synthesis_Procedure: Ba1 − x SrxFe11Cr1O19 hexaferrites with different concentrations (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8) were synthesized via co-precipitation technique. The precursors used for the preparation of hexaferrites were Ba(NO3)2, Fe(NO3)3·9H2O, Cr(NO3)3·6H2O, Sr(NO3)2·6H2O, KOH and distilled water. Firstly, the stoichiometric amounts of nitrates were dissolved in 100 ml of distilled water. Then, the starting mixture containing nitrates were added drop wise in the 100 ml solution of precipitating catalyst KOH . Precipitates were formed by heating the solutions at 70 °C under stirring at a hotplate for 2 h. The obtained precipitates were then collected and washed several times before getting dried at 100 °C overnight in oven. Afterward, the obtained dried powders were annealed at 1000 °C for 12 h. Finally, pellets were formed from the annealed powders by applying a pressure of 5 tons/cm2 followed by 6 h sintering at 1200 °C.

Synthesis_Procedure: Precursor sols of BaNixFe12−xO19 (x = 0.0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 and 1.0) were prepared by gel–combustion method. Aqueous solutions of Ba, Ni and Fe nitrates were prepared, starting from barium nitrate Ba(NO3)2 (≥99%, Merck), nickel nitrate hexahydrate Ni(NO3)2·6H2O (≥99.999%, Merck) and iron (III) nitrate nonahydrate Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (≥99.99%, Merck) and citric acid (≥99.95%, Merck). The required amount of citric acid, dissolved in distilled water, corresponding to the molar ratio citric acid: nitrate (CA/NO3− ) = 1.0, was added to the cations aqueous solution, at ~75 °C. The citrate–nitrate precursor sols of BaNixFe12−xO19 were heated at about 100 °C, in order to evaporate the water and to obtain the gel precursors. BaNixFe12−xO19 powders were produced by the auto–combustion process of the as–prepared citrate–nitrate gel. We chose a ratio CA/NO3- = 1 considering that if excessive HNO3 is used (CA/NO3-<1), the combustion is more violent due to the presence of NH4NO3. After auto–combustion of the gels at ~400 °C, the resultant powders were fired at 1250 °C, 2 h in air, in order to obtain single phase powders. The as–prepared powders were used to prepare ceramics by two sintering methods such as: classic sintering and spark plasma sintering. Synthesis_Procedure: The investigated samples BaFe11(Sn0.5Mg0.5)1−xNdxO19 (x = 0, 0.5, 1) were synthesized via co-precipitation technique. The stoichiometric quantity of barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)2, iron(III) chloride (FeCl3), Tin (IV) chloride SnCl4, magnesium chloride (MgCl2), and neodymium oxide (Nd2O3)) was assorted into a suitable volume of deionized water. Neodymium oxide (Nd2O3) was not soluble in water; to make Nd2O3 soluble, it was dissolved in HNO3 solution for the completion of neodymium nitrate [15]. To get a homogenous solution, continuously stirring was adopted, together with simultaneous heating at 70 °C for 1 h. A solution of 1.5 M NaOH was poured, dropwise, to optimize the solution pH to 13 during the precipitation process. Moreover, the aqueous solutions were stirred for 0.5 h to achieve an appropriate homogeneity and a constant pH. After that, the precipitate-containing aqueous solutions were washed and filtered by deionized water until a solution pH reached 7. Further, the brownish filtered suspensions were heated at 150 °C (12 h) to evaporate the water, followed by grinding, thus producing a fine powder. Subsequently, the dried precursors were sintered at 900 °C for 4 h at ambient atmosphere, thus providing the hexagonal phase.

Synthesis_Procedure: The starting materials used in this work were SrCO3 (99% purity), La2O3 (99% purity), Fe2O3 (99% purity), NiO (99% purity) and ZrO2 (99% purity). They were used as such without further treatment. The standard ceramic method were used to prepare the Sr–La hexaferrites with nominal compositions of Sr0.7La0.3Fe12.0−2x(NiZr)xO19 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5). The starting powders of SrCO3, La2O3, Fe2O3, NiO and ZrO2 were weighted in accordance with the ratios of the chemical composition. The starting materials were wet-mixed in a ball mill at a rotate speed of 80 rpm for 10 h. After that, the mixed powders were dried in a drying oven in the air, and then calcined in a muffle furnace at 1260 °C for 2.0 h in air. After that, the calcined samples were shattered to particles less than 60 µm by a vibration mill. Finally, to relieve the stress, the shattered particles were annealed in a muffle furnace at 750 °C for 1.5 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: BaFe12−2xCexZnxO19 (x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.3) nano-crystalline powders were synthesized using citrate nitrate auto-combustion route. Synthesized compositions were designated as BFO (x = 0), BFCZO1 (x = 0.1) and BFCZO3 (x = 0.3). Barium carbonate (99% purity, Sigma Aldrich), ammonium ceric nitrate (99% purity, Qualikems, India), Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (98% purity, Fisher Scientific), Zn(NO3)2·9H2O (96% purity, Fisher Scientific) and citric acid (99.5% purity, Loba Chemie, India) were used as the starting materials. Stoichiometric amount of BaCO3 was weighed and dissolved in dilute nitric acid (1 : 4) to obtain Ba(NO3)2 followed by heating at 413 K till complete dryness. Ceric ammonium nitrate, barium nitrate, zinc nitrate, ferric nitrate and citric acid were then dissolved in double distilled water separately to make an aqueous transparent solution. All the prepared aqueous nitrate solutions were then added to the citric acid solution keeping the citrate to nitrate molar ratio (C/ N) ~0.3 for controlled and smooth combustion.23 The final mixed solution was then heated continuously at 473 K with continuous slow stirring. During heating, all the excess water evaporated, and the mass became viscous and turned into a gel. The gel slowly foamed followed by ignition and burnt into ash within a very short time-period. The ash was then collected and grounded using agate mortar-pestle. The ground powder was then calcined at 1373 K for 4 h in air. The calcined powders were then mixed with 2% PVA and pressed uniaxially under a load of 50 kN to form cylindrical pellets of diameter ~12 mm and thickness ~1.5 mm. The pellets were sintered in five steps using an electrical furnace (Lenton, made in UK). In the first step, the temperature was raised to 773 K with a heating rate of 2 K min−1 and held at this temperature for 1 h to remove the binder. The temperature was then raised to 1573 K (heating rate 5 K min−1) and held there for 6 h and finally cooled down to the room temperature.

Synthesis_Procedure: Strontium hexaferrite (SrM) was prepared by the citrate route. Analytical grade iron powder (VWR Prolabo), strontium carbonate SrCO3 (Merck, Technipur), and citric acid monohydrate C6H8O7•H2O (VWR) were used as starting materials for the synthesis of the citrate precursor mixture. The Sr/Fe ratio was adjusted to 1:11, whereas the ratio of metal ions/citric acid was set to 1:1. The reagents were mixed in deionized water and stirred for 5 h under reflux conditions. Aqueous ammonia was added until a dark green, clear solution was obtained (pH = 8) and the water was subsequently removed at 95 °C. The resulting dry solid was ground to a fine powder and pre-calcined at a temperature T1 between 300 and 500 °C for 2 h in air. A second calcination step was performed at T2 between 600 and 700 °C for 2 h in air. For surfactant-assisted ball milling studies, a larger batch of SrM powder was prepared via the citrate route and split into 10 g portions for milling experiments. To ensure complete SrM formation for larger powder quantities, each batch was calcined three times between 650 and 700 °C with homogenization between the calcination steps. Finally, ferrite powder milling was performed in a planetary ball mill Fritsch Pulverisette 5 in a 60 cm3 POM milling vessel using zirconia grinding media with a diameter of 0.5 mm and a mass ratio of powder/zirconia/liquid as 1/10/ 2. Milling experiments were performed in water or n-heptane at 400 rpm at least four times for 5 min. In aqueous media, the following surfactants (relative to ferrite powder) were added: (1) 0.5 wt% PEG6000 (Alfa Aesar) as nonionic surfactant at pH = 7, (2) 0.5 wt% of sodium dodecyl sulfate SDS (AppliChem) as anionic surfactant at pH = 3 using acetic acid, and (3) 0.5 wt% cetyltrimethylammonium bromide CTAB (Fluka) as cationic surfactant at pH = 10 using sodium hydroxide. A dispersion 0.5 wt% oleic acid was used as surfactant in n-heptane. To test the stability of SrF powder under reducing conditions, the ferrite powder was annealed in a tube furnace in an Ar/5% H2 gas atmosphere at temperatures from 350 to 500 °C for 2 h with 5 K/min heating and cooling rate.

The Sr/Fe ratio was adjusted to 1:11, whereas the ratio of metal ions/citric acid was set to 1:1. The reagents were mixed in deionized water and stirred for 5 h under reflux conditions. Aqueous ammonia was added until a dark green, clear solution was obtained (pH = 8) and the water was subsequently removed at 95 °C. The resulting dry solid was ground to a fine powder and pre-calcined at a temperature T1 between 300 and 500 °C for 2 h in air. A second calcination step was performed at T2 between 600 and 700 °C for 2 h in air. For surfactant-assisted ball milling studies, a larger batch of SrM powder was prepared via the citrate route and split into 10 g portions for milling experiments. To ensure complete SrM formation for larger powder quantities, each batch was calcined three times between 650 and 700 °C with homogenization between the calcination steps. Finally, ferrite powder milling was performed in a planetary ball mill Fritsch Pulverisette 5 in a 60 cm3 POM milling vessel using zirconia grinding media with a diameter of 0.5 mm and a mass ratio of powder/zirconia/liquid as 1/10/ 2. Milling experiments were performed in water or n-heptane at 400 rpm at least four times for 5 min. In aqueous media, the following surfactants (relative to ferrite powder) were added: (1) 0.5 wt% PEG6000 (Alfa Aesar) as nonionic surfactant at pH = 7, (2) 0.5 wt% of sodium dodecyl sulfate SDS (AppliChem) as anionic surfactant at pH = 3 using acetic acid, and (3) 0.5 wt% cetyltrimethylammonium bromide CTAB (Fluka) as cationic surfactant at pH = 10 using sodium hydroxide. A dispersion 0.5 wt% oleic acid was used as surfactant in n-heptane. To test the stability of SrF powder under reducing conditions, the ferrite powder was annealed in a tube furnace in an Ar/5% H2 gas atmosphere at temperatures from 350 to 500 °C for 2 h with 5 K/min heating and cooling rate.

Synthesis_Procedure: Ball milling was used to prepare Sr1-xRExFe12O19 (x = 0, 0.1) hexaferrite precursor powders from analytical grade SrCO3, Fe2O3, RE2O3 (RE: La, Ce, Tb) starting powders. Stoichiometric ratios of the starting powders were mixed and charged into the zirconia vessels of Fritsch Pulverisette 7 ball mill. Wet milling of the powder mixture in an acetone bath was performed for 16 h at a rotational speed of 250 rpm. The resulting powder was left to dry at room temperature. Diskshape pellets of 1.25 cm diameter and ~ 1 mm thickness were then compacted under a force of 5 tons. The disks were then sintered in air at 1200 °C for 2 h in a zirconium oxide crucible. Sol–gel auto-combustion method was also used to prepare the above-mentioned SrM hexaferrites. The stoichiometric amounts of high-purity Fe(NO3)3.9H2O, Sr(NO3)2 and rareearth nitrates were dissolved in deionized water under magnetic stirring. Then, citric acid (C6H8O7.H2O) was added into the metal nitrate solution with citric acid/Fe molar ratio of 1:3. Ethylene glycol was then added with citric acid/ ethylene glycol mass ratio of 2:3), and the pH of the solution was adjusted to 7 by adding ammonia dropwise. The reaction mixture was then evaporated at 80 °C on a hot plate, and the high viscosity gel was left at room temperature for 24 h. Auto-combustion occurred by heating the gel at 450 °C, giving a fine loose powder, which was subsequently calcined at 650 °C to remove the organic materials. Disk-shape pellets of the powder were then prepared by compaction under a force of 5 tons. Since sol–gel method was known to be suitable for synthesis of hexaferrites at lower temperatures compared with ball milling, the disks were sintered in air for 2 h at different temperatures (900 °C, 1100 °C and 1200 °C) to investigate the effect of heat treatment on the structural and magnetic properties of the compounds.

Synthesis_Procedure: The standard ceramic method were used to prepare the M-type Ca-Sr hexaferrites with nominal compositions of Sr0.8-xCa0.2PrxFe12.0-x(Bi0.5Co0.5)xO19 (0.0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5).
