Synthesis_Procedure: The powders of Ba(NiZn)x/2Co1−xTiFe10O19 (BNZCTM) (x = 0.2 to 0.4 in step of 0.1) were synthesized by a sol-gel combustion technique. The appropriate stoichiometric Fe(NO3)3•9H2O (AR), Ba(NO3)2 (AR), Ti(OC4H9)4 (AR), Co(NO3)2•6H2O (AR), Zn(NO3)2•6H2O (AR), and Ni(NO3)2•6H2O were dissolved in 50 mL deionized water with magnetic stirring. After solutes were completely dissolved, the 0.065-mol citric acid (AR) was added into the solution and then entirely dissolved. The ammonia solution (AR) was added by dropwise to adjust the pH value to 7. With magnetic stirring, the adjusted solution was heated up to 100 °C to obtain dried gel. With continued heating, the dried gel would burn up in a self-propagating combustion manner and some powders could be gained. These powders were heated up to 450 °C with a heating rate of 5 °C/min and pre-calcined for 4 h, then heated up to 1100 °C with a speed of 3 °C/min and calcined for 4 h, and finally down to 800 °C at 3 °C/min and maintained for 4 h to obtain the BNZCTM powders.

Synthesis_Procedure: SrFe12-2xZnxSnxO19 (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2) samples were prepared via conventional ceramic method. The raw materials required for samples preparation are Fe2O3 (Aladdin, 99.9%), SrCO3 (Aladdin, 99.95%), SnO2 (Aladdin, 99.9%) and ZnO (Aladdin, 99.9%). Synthesis_Procedure: Dy–Ni co-substituted M-type Sr ferrite was synthesized through a solid-state reaction method. The chemical formula of the specimens was Sr1-xDyxFe12-xNixO19 (x = 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, and 0.05). Analytically purified powders of SrCO3 (99 %), Fe2O3 (99 %), NiO (99 %), and Dy2O3 (99.9 %) were used as raw materials, SrCO3 and Fe2O3 were from Chron Chemicals, NiO and Dy2O3 were produced by Aladdin. To begin, the raw materials were meticulously weighed and added to a ball mill in the appropriate molar ratios. Subsequently, the mixture was thoroughly ground, and deionized water was gradually added to form a slurry. The slurry was subjected to ball milling for a duration of 2 h. Upon completion, the resulting slurry was transferred to a container and placed in a drying oven for dehydration. The dried powder was then sieved to obtain a fine powder. Next, the powder was introduced into a muffle furnace and subjected to sintering at a temperature of 1190 ◦ C, resulting in the formation of calcined powder. The calcined powder was subsequently subjected to secondary ball milling for 17 h, producing a secondary slurry. The secondary slurry was driedin a container toobtain a secondary dry powder. The secondary dry powder was further processed by grinding and granulating in a mortar, with the addition of a specific mass fraction of PVA. This process yielded granulated powder. The granulated powder was weighed to a predetermined amount and poured into a mold. It was then pressed using a powder tablet press to obtain pressed samples. Finally, the compacted samples were positioned within a furnace and subjected to sintering at 900 ◦ C, resulting in the production of the final ferrite product, which was subsequently used for further experimental investigations. The sample preparation flow chart is depicted in Fig. 2.

Synthesis_Procedure: The precursor solution was prepared with 80.776 g of Fe (NO3)3 ⋅ 9H2O, a specific amount of Sr (NO3)2, and a corresponding amount of Sm (NO3)3 ⋅ 6H2O. These were dissolved in deionized water to obtain a solution containing Fe3+ , Sr2+ , and Sm3+ . The precursor solution can be expressed as Sm3+ : Sr2+ : Fe3+ = x: 1: (12-x) (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, and 0.3) (all ratios are molar ratios). To prepare porous SrFe12O19 powders, different contents of KCl were also dissolved in the above precursor solution. Table 1 lists the different formulations of various precursor solutions. The precursor solutions were ultrasonically stirred for 1 h to obtain a homogeneous solution. The concentration of Fe3+ in the solution was maintained at 0.2 mol/L. The chemical reagents Fe (NO3)3⋅9H2O, Sr(NO3)2, Sm(NO3)3⋅6H2O, and KCl were analytically pure. The ultrasonic atomizer was placed in the prepared precursor solution, which was atomized into small droplets at a frequency of 1.7 MHz. The droplets were introduced into a pyrolysis furnace with three temperature zones, with air as the carrier atmosphere, at a flow rate of 4 L/min. The first stage was the drying zone, in which the temperature was 300 ◦ C, the solvent pure water was evaporated, and solid particles were precipitated from the droplets. The second stage was the decomposition zone, in which the temperature was 600 ◦ C, and the nitrate decomposed to form the corresponding oxide. Synthesis_Procedure: The auto-combustion sol-gel technique is employed to create M-type hexaferrite doped with various elements. This synthetic method generates ferrite nanoparticles that offer favourable qualities including easy preparation, minimal equipment requirements, notable chemical uniformity, heightened powder purity, and a crystalline structure. Different Nitrates salts such as Strontium nitrate Sr(NO3)2 (99.5 %, Purity), Ferric nitrate nonahydrate Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O (99–101 %, Purity), Praseodymium nitrate Pr(NO3)3⋅xH2O (99.9 %, Purity), Aluminium nitrate Al (NO3)3⋅xH2O (98.5 %, Purity), Anhydrous citric acid C6H8O7, ethylene glycol C2H6O2 and ammonia solution obtained from central drug house (P) Ltd are used in the preparations. The chemical route followed by the equations are: (1-X).Sr(NO3)2 + X.Pr(NO3)2 + 10Fe(NO3)2 + 2Al(NO3)2 + C6H8O7 + NH4OH → Sr1xPrxAl2Fe10O19 + NH4NO3 + CO2 + H2O Achieving a transparent solution necessitates 20–25 ml of double distilled water and continuous stirring to completely dissolve the metal nitrates in a stoichiometric ratio, provided in Table 1. Citric acid serves as a chelating agent, preventing the formation of hydroxylated molecules by forming complexes with metal ions. Water-soluble salts act as initiators due to their capacity to function as low-temperature NO3 oxidants. The mixture’s pH is adjusted with ammonia to bring it within the desired range of 8–8.5. The solution’s pH has a role in regulating the sample particle’s size [32]. Nanoparticles are generated, and agglomeration is prevented by employing ethylene glycol as a surfactant. Introducing ethylene glycol into the mixture at 80 ◦ C boosts heat evolution and reduces ignition temperature, thus facilitating the synthesis of single-phase hexaferrite (illustrated in Fig. 3). This additive also helps manage solution viscosity and control cation-cation exchange rates, contributing to the formation of a uniform polymer network [33]. The powder obtained after the release of gases at temperatures ranging from 80 ◦ C to 100 ◦ C undergoes calcination at 1100 ◦ C for 4 h. This calcined powder is utilized for both the structural and magnetic analyses of the specimens.

Synthesis_Procedure: 400 ml of de-ionized water was employed as a solvent for dissolving stoichiometric amounts of calcium, barium, and iron nitrate salts to yield a uniform mixture. The molar ratio of barium, calcium, and iron was 0.8:0.2:12 in the BaCaM compound. Then, the stoichiometric amount of zirconyl nitrate, cobalt nitrates, and citric acid was incorporated into the solution. Furthermore, stoichiometric amounts of various salts were employed to synthesize different compositions of Ba0.8Ca0.2Fe12-2xCoxZrxO19 as shown in Table 1. Gradually adding ammonium hydroxide helped to control the reaction mixture’s pH. The solution was then placed under perpetual heating via magnetic stirring for 5–6 h at 90–95 ◦ C. Evaporation of excessive water leads to the formation of viscous gel. The viscous gel was heated for 1–2 h at 200 to 250 ◦ C to initiate the auto-ignition process in the hot air oven. During the auto-combustion process, porous material was formed [19]. Using a mortar and pestle, this extremely amorphous substance was crushed into a fine powder. To remove impurities and acquire crystalline Ba0.8Ca0.2Fe12-2xCoxZrxO19 phase, this powder was heated at 900 ◦ C for 6 h. These samples were then characterized by FTIR, VSM, Raman, and Impedance Analyzer, and X-ray diffractometer. Fig. 1 shows the process flowchart for Ba0.8Ca0.2Fe12-2xCoxZrxO19 synthesis and characterization.

Here, metal nitrates are used as oxidants. All the solution of metal nitrates and fuel were mixed properly to form homogeneous yellow brown colour aqueous solution. Synthesis_Procedure: Sol–gel auto-combustion method was employed for the synthesis of Ba1-xCoxFe12 O19 x=(0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6) nanoparticles. Flowchart for the preparation of material is shown in Fig. 1. To prepare 0.4 M solutions, deionized water was mixed with stoichiometric amounts of Ba(NO3)2⋅4H2O, citric acid C6H8O7⋅H2O, aqueous ammonia (NH4OH), cobalt nitrate Co(NO3)2⋅6H2O, and iron nitrate Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O in different beakers. To attain the desired pH, a 2 M ammonia solution was used until a pH of around 7 was reached. The solutions were heated and mixed at 70 °C for 4 h. The beakers were removed from the hot plate, once the fluffy gel had formed. Beakers were put in an oven and set at a temperature of 150 °C to dry the gel. After drying, the gel was gently ground using an agate mortar and pestle. The ground samples were inserted into the crucibles. The samples were sintered in an inert gas oven at 900 °C for 9 h. The samples were then ground into fine powder and stored in glass vials.

Synthesis_Procedure: Different polycrystalline samples of BaFe12−2xIrxCoxO19 for x varying from 0 to 0.8 were prepared by sintering of metallic oxides. The synthesis was divided into two steps. After calcination at 800°C for 2 h at air according to the reaction BaCO3 + (6 − x)Fe2O3 → BaFe2O4 + (5 − x)Fe2O3 + CO2, IrO2 and CoO oxides were added. The mixture was grinded and dried, compressed into pellets and putted in evacuated quartz tubes which have been finally subjected to a thermal treatment at 1100°C for 48 h. According to the reaction BaFe2O4 + (5 − x)Fe2O3 + xIrO2 + xCoO → BaFe12−2xIrxCoxO19 substituted M-ferrites have been obtained at relative low temperature. Unfortunately, Fe2O3 and spinel CoFe2O4 impurities were present under these conditions. They could be avoided by introducing a higher content of barium. A barium excess required in order to obtain pure phase of substituted Ti/Co M-Barium hexaferrites, has already been referred [4].

Synthesis_Procedure: A mixture of 99% pure nonmagnetic α-Fe2O3 and BaCO3 powders were used as starting materials for production of BaFe12O19 by conventional sinter method and mechanochemical reaction in a high-energy ball milling. The molar ratio of α-Fe2O3 to BaCO3 was 6:1 in the mixture. In the conventional sinter process, the mixture was sintered from room temperature to 1000◦ C. In the mechanochemical reaction process, the mixture was milled in a mill firstly and annealed under ambient pressure in a temperature ranging from room temperature to 1000◦ C. A stainless vial filled with stainless balls having diameter of 5–15mm was used as the milling medium. The mass of the mixture was 7g and the balls-to-powder mass ratio was 15:1. The mixture was milled under air ambient without any additives (dry milling). In the glycin–nitrate process, the starting materials used were 99% pure iron nitrate(Fe(NO3)3·9H2O), barium nitrate(Ba(NO3)2), glycin and distilled water. Appropriate amount of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O and Ba(NO3)2, in a Fe/Ba molar ratio of 12 were dissolved in the required amount of distilled water. The molar ratio of glycin to total moles of nitrate ions was adjusted at 1.5:1. The precursor powders were annealed under ordinary pressure ambient in a temperature ranging from room temperature to 1000◦ C. These samples were pressed into disk (under pressure of 0.2GPa) and sintered for 2h in air atmosphere in a temperature ranging from 700 to 1000◦ C.

Synthesis_Procedure: We have adopted the conventional sol–gel method based on polymeric precursor route for synthesizing the n-BFO. In this method, reagent grade chemicals such as Ba(NO3)2·4H2O, Fe(NO3)2·9H2O and citric acid (according to their equal cation molar ratio) were taken as the precursor materials and weighted according to the stoichiometric ratio. First barium nitrate and iron nitrate compounds were dissolved in deionized water and they mixed with citric acid solution. To this precursor mixture ethylene glycol was added (few drops) while continuously stirring the solution. In order to maintain the good chemical homogeneity by high degree chelation of metallic cations, we added NH3 to get the pH value 12 of the starting precursor solution. The solvent was evaporated directly in the temperatures range between 75 and 150 °C using on a hot plate until a thick solution and then solid resin was formed. The resin was calcinated at temperatures 950 °C for 2 h duration to get the nanoparticles.

Synthesis_Procedure: We have adopted the conventional sol–gel method based on polymeric precursor route for synthesizing the n-BFO. In this method, reagent grade chemicals such as Ba(NO3)2·4H2O, Fe(NO3)2·9H2O and citric acid (according to their equal cation molar ratio) were taken as the precursor materials and weighted according to the stoichiometric ratio. First barium nitrate and iron nitrate compounds were dissolved in deionized water and they mixed with citric acid solution. To this precursor mixture ethylene glycol was added (few drops) while continuously stirring the solution. In order to maintain the good chemical homogeneity by high degree chelation of metallic cations, we added NH3 to get the pH value 12 of the starting precursor solution. The solvent was evaporated directly in the temperatures range between 75 and 150 °C using on a hot plate until a thick solution and then solid resin was formed. The resin was calcinated at temperatures 950 °C for 2 h duration to get the nanoparticles.

Synthesis_Procedure: In series 1, desired metal nitrates in appropriate ratios were taken in minimum amount of distilled water followed by the addition of ethylene glycol (50% by volume of solution) and stirred until a homogeneous mixture was observed. The solution was heated on the water bath at 80–90 °C for the formation of gel. The gel so obtained was further heated at 250 °C for 2 h. Self combustion occurred and a dry fluffy mass was obtained. The material was finely ground. The final sintering was done at 850 °C for 6 h in a PID controlled box furnace where the heating and cooling rates were maintained at 20 °C/min [21]. In series 2, stoichiometric amount of ferric nitrate was converted into ferric hydroxide by the addition of ammonia. These precipitates were filtered, washed several times with distilled water and dissolved in hot citric acid solution (citric acid: total metal 1.1:1), followed by addition of desired amounts of BaCO3 (H2O2 was added to decompose BaCO3 and solution was heated below 100 °C to expel out CO2 and excess H2O2). Dopant ions in the form of their nitrates and ethylene glycol (10% by volume of solution) were added to the hot reaction mixture. A few drops of HNO3 were added to maintain the acidic environment (pH ~ 3). The contents were stirred for 2 h and heated slowly until a highly viscous residue was obtained which was heated for another 2 h at 150 °C. The gel formed was ignited calcinated at 800 °C in furnace [22]. The purity of the ferrites was checked by FT-IR [23], XRD (space group P63/mmc, JCPDS file number 84-0757) and EDS [24].

Synthesis_Procedure: A self combustion method has been adopted in order to synthesize BaM. Hydrated metal salts viz. Ba(NO3)2, Co(NO3)2·6H2O, ZrO(NO3)2·6H2O, and Fe(NO3)3·9H2O were employed as starting material for the synthesis. In this synthesis, stoichiometric amounts of desired metal nitrate solutions were mixed with citric acid solution under constant stirring. Total metal ion to citric acid ratio was kept constant as 1:1.1. Nitrogen containing compound urea solution was added to metal nitrate and citric acid solution and metal ion to urea ratio was maintained as (metal ion: urea) 1:2. Nitric acid was added according to the volume of solution to maintain acidic conditions. The obtained solution was evaporated at 80 °C and continuous evaporation leads to the formation of polymeric resin. The obtained polymeric resin was further dried at 150 °C for 2 h to remove excess water. A highly porous intermediate which is prepared with urea was observed. This intermediate sample was grounded and calcined at 800 °C for 4 h to obtain nanocrystalline BaCoxZrxFe(122x)O19 powder. The final powder was ground in pestle mortar to form a fine powder for characterization (see Scheme 1).

Synthesis_Procedure: Polycrystalline Ba0.95Y0.05Fe12−xMnxO19 compounds with x = 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 were fabricated by the solid-state reaction route. Sigma-Aldrich chemicals including BaCO3, Y2O3, Fe2O3 and MnCO3 (purity of 99.9%) combined with nominal compositions of Ba0.95Y0.05Fe12−xMnxO19 (hereafter labeled BaYFe12−xMnxO19) were mixed and ground by using a high-energy ball mill (SPEX SamplePrep) and stainless-steel grinding media. The raw materials, agate ball and deionized water with mass ratio of 1:1.5:1.2 were mixed together in agate jar to ball-mill for 8 h. The slurries were dried in an oven for 12 h and then pre-sintered at 950 °C for 24 h with the heating rate of 5 °C/min. For better homogenization, the pre-sintered samples were manual grinded before the second ballmilling for 8 h. After that, PVA solution with a mass ratio of 5% was added for granulation. The samples were pressed into disc-shape with diameter of 12 mm and thickness of 1 mm and then sintered at 1160 °C for 16 h in furnace.

Synthesis_Procedure: Six barium ferrite samples including a pristine sample (A) were synthesized by the sol–gel auto-combustion technique. The BaFe12−xBixO19 samples with x = 0.1 and 0.5 are respectively referred to as B and C. Samples coded D, E, and F are Ba1−xFe12−xBixCuxO19 with x = 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 respectively. Bi and Bi-Cu ions were introduced by adding bismuth(III) nitrate pentahydrate (Bi (NO3)3·5H2O) and copper(II) nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2·3H2O) in the reaction between iron(III) nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3- ·9H2O) and barium nitrate (Ba(NO3)3). The starting materials were dissolved in 30 mL of deionized water. Then, 1.441 g of citric acid was added to the solution and completely dissolved under constant stirring. Citric acid is a fuel in the gel combustion commonly used for barium ferrite syntheses (Mohammed et al., 2019; Jasrotia et al., 2019). The pH of the solution was adjusted to 7 by adding ammonium hydroxide (NH4OH) solution (25%). After heating at 90 °C for 230 min, the solution turned into a viscous gel. The next heating step at 150 °C for 190 min enabled the gel combustion resulting in a brown product. The ground product was subsequently heated in a furnace at 450 °C for 2 h and at 1050 °C for 3 h with a heating rate of 4.5 °C/min.

Synthesis_Procedure: Strontium hexaferrite nanoparticles are prepared using the chemical sol–gel route. Stoichiometric amount of Fe(NO3)3 was dissolved in distilled water and quantitatively precipitated by concentrated ammonia in solution. Zinc nitrate, niobium nitrate and strontium nitrate with an atomic ratio Fe:Sr=11.6:1 were added, and a homogeneous transparent solution was obtained in a few seconds. This solution, to which stoichiometric amount of ethylene glycol was added, was slowly evaporated at 60° C until a high viscous residual was formed; then, a gel was developed during heating at 180° C. The gel was annealed at temperatures between 200° C and 1000° C for 5h at a rate of 4.5° C/min. Before annealing, the gel was preheated to 450° C using the same rates to decompose the organic precursor.

Synthesis_Procedure: Appropriate amounts of BaCO3, Fe2O3 and La2O3 powders of high purity were weighed and mixed to prepare (Ba1·xLax)·nFe2O3 (0.0rxr1.0 and 1rnr6) samples having various Fe/(Ba+La) ratios between 2 and 12. The mixed powder was put into the melted ammonium nitrate. The solution was mixed on a hot plate with magnetic stirrer until the liquid phases disappear. Before grinding in an agate mortar for 15 min, small amount of isopropyl alcohol was added to make wet grinding. The precursor was calcinated at 450 1C for 5 h to remove possible organic compounds. Then, it was again ground for 15 min with isopropyl alcohol and dried, pelletized under the pressure of 200 MPa. In our previous publication, it was shown that pelletizing before calcinations may improve the hard phase fraction and thus the magnetization of the material [23]. The pressed disk-shaped pellets (diameter 16 mm, and thickness 3 mm) were sintered at 800–1200 1C for 2 h in air and cooled in the furnace. Finally, another grinding process took place for 15 min to obtain the samples in powder form which were washed with HCl and measured in VSM.

Before grinding in an agate mortar for 15 min, small amount of isopropyl alcohol was added to make wet grinding. The precursor was calcinated at 450 1C for 5 h to remove possible organic compounds. The pressed disk-shaped pellets (diameter 16 mm, and thickness 3 mm) were sintered at 800–1200 1C for 2 h in air and cooled in the furnace. Synthesis_Procedure: The M-type barium ferrites (Ba(CoTi)xFe11.8−2xO19) were prepared by the traditional solid-state method. The raw materials, BaCO3, Fe2O3, Co3O4 and TiO2 (high purity) were mixed by the molar ratio and ball-milled for 12 h, then dried and calcinated at 1200 1C in air for 2 h. Various contents of BaCu(B2O5) ceramic additive (1–4 wt%), which was prepared by the way reported by Sahn Nahm [12], were added to the powder and ball-milled for 12 h again. The resulting powder was pressed into pellets and toroidal samples with 15 wt% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as a binder and were sintered at various temperatures from 850 to 950 1C for 4 h. In order to investigate the compatibility of BCB-added barium ferrite and silver paste, a ferrite sheet with an Ag electrode was prepared by tape casting and co-fired at 900 1C.

Synthesis_Procedure: The hexaferrite magnetic powders and magnets were synthesized using the ceramic process. In the present investigation, the SrCO3 (97% purity), La2O3 (99% purity), Fe2O3 (98% purity) and ZnO (99% purity) were used as starting materials. Powders of the starting materials were accurately weighed according to the composition of Sr0.70−xCaxLa0.30Fe11.75Zn0.25O19, where the calcium content (x) varies from 0 to 0.70 with about 0.10 increment. And then, the starting materials were charged in a ball mill together with hardened steel balls with a diameter of 8 mm. Synthesis_Procedure: In the present work, SrAl4Fe8O19 was synthesized by three different methods, i.e., solid-state (SS), co-precipitation (CP), and sol–gel autocombustion (SG) methods. The description and flow chart (as shown in Scheme 1) of the synthesis processes are as follows: 2.1. Solid-state method To prepare SrAl4Fe8O19 ferrite using the solid-state method, SrCO3, Al2O3, and Fe2O3 were used as raw materials. All the raw materials were purchased from Loba Chemie Pvt. Ltd., India, with a 99.9% assay. Accordingly, the stoichiometric composition of raw materials was weighed at Sr: (Fe + Al) = 1:12. The powders were charged in a zirconia jar. It was subjected to a wet planetary ball mill (Insmart Systems, Model: MBM-07, Hyderabad, India) with a 1:1 mixture of DI water and IPA (Isopropyl alcohol) solution. The ball-to-raw powder ratio was kept at 8:1 and milled at 400 rpm for 6 h. The dried powder was calcined at 1250 ◦ C for 4 h to prepare single-phase SrAl4Fe8O19 ferrite. The dried calcined powder was granulated with a 3 % PVA (polyvinyl alcohol) binder. The granulated powder was further uniaxially pressed at six tonnes/cm2 to produce cylindrical pellets. The pellets were further sintered (with a heating rate of 3 ◦ C/min) at 1250 ◦ C for 2 h. 2.2. Co-precipitation method To synthesis SrAl4Fe8O19 ferrite by co-precipitation method, strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2], aluminum nitrate [Al(NO3)3⋅9H2O], and iron nitrate [Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O] were taken in the stoichiometric ratio. All the raw materials were purchased from Loba Chemie Pvt. Ltd., India, with a 99.9% assay. The molar ratio of Fe: Sr was maintained at 12:1. The solutions of the raw materials were formed with a small amount of distilled water. This solution was continuously stirred at 50 ◦ C temperature. NH4OH solution was added up dropwise to the solution and maintained the pH of the solution by 11. NH4OH solution act as a precipitating agent in the solution. After maintaining the pH of the solution, the sample was left for 3 h for stirring to control the homogeneity of the mixture. After 3 h, precipitates were cleaned through DI water and dried at 100 ◦ C in the oven for 5 h. The dried precipitate powder was ground and kept for calcination at 1100 ◦ C for 2 h to get the single-phase SrAl4Fe8O19 ferrite. 3 % PVA was added to the ground powder. Granulated powder was pressed at six tonnes/cm2 to produce cylindrical. The formed pellet was sintered at (with a heating rate of 3 ◦ C/min) 1250 ◦ C for 2 h in an open atmosphere. 2.3. Sol-gel auto-combustion method The stoichiometric ratios of strontium nitrate [Sr(NO3)2], aluminum nitrate [Al(NO3)3⋅9H2O], iron nitrate [Fe(NO3)3⋅9H2O], & citric acid [C6H8O7⋅H2O] were dissolved in deionized water to prepare SrAl4 Fe8O19 ferrite by the sol gel auto-combustion method. The molar ratio of metal cations and citric acid was 1:1 in the solution. The pH of the solution was adjusted to 7 with the addition of an ammonia solution. Then, the solution was kept at 80 ◦ C temperature for converting into a gel. Later, the gel exploded and formed into burnt powder by the selfpropagating combustion method. The burnt powder was calcined at 1100◦ C for 2 h to get the Sr-hexaferrite phase. The calcined powders were pressed at six tonnes/cm2 and formed the pellet, using PVA as a binder. The pellets were further sintered at (with a heating rate of 3 ◦ C/ min) 1250 ◦ C for 2 h.

Citric acid (C6H8O7) was then added to the prepared aqueous solution to chelate Ba2+ and Fe3+ ions in the solution because among all other fuels citric acid has better complexing ability, low ignition temperature (i.e. 200–250°C) and controlled combustion reaction with nitrates. After optimizing the pH of the mixed solution it was kept at 8 by adding ammonia solution. The mixed solution was evaporated to dryness by heating at 100°C on a hot plate with continuous stirring and finally formed a very viscous brown gel. This viscous brown gel was ignited by increasing the temperature up to 150°C and the loose powder of the samples was obtained. Finally, using the TGA- DTA data analysis (not shown here) the as-burnt powder when sintered at 900°C for 8 h gives the nanosize nature of the aluminium substituted barium hexaferrite evidenced by X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy.

Synthesis_Procedure: The pure phase Strontium Hexaferrite, SrFe12O19 was prepared using a low cost chemical based citrate precursor sol-gel method. Chemicals used in this process were of high purity standards namely, Sr (NO3)2, Fe (NO3)3 (Alfa Aesar, 99.9% purity). For chelation during synthesis, Citric acid was used. The stoichiometric ratio of citric acid to metal cations was maintained to be 1:3 during synthesis. At first, an exact stoichiometric proportion of chemical nitrates was weighed and dissolved into separate beakers containing a minimal amount of deionized water. Thereafter, these aqueous solutions of iron nitrate and strontium nitrate were poured into the beaker containing citric acid solution. Further pH of this final solution was shifted to 7, with a drop wise addition of Ammonia. Finally, this solution was heated under constant stirring at temperature 80 ℃ on a hot plate stirrer for (3-4) hours, till a viscous gel-like substance is obtained. The viscous gel was then kept in a hot air oven chamber at 120 ℃ throughout the night to dry. When the temperature in the hot air oven was increased to 250 ℃ for 30 minutes, gel swelled into foam, guided by a self-propagating combustion reaction. Finally, we obtain a voluminous like ash powder, which is further ground to fine powders with Mortar and Pestle. The powdered nanomaterials were then transferred into a microprocessor based annealing furnace, in alumina crucibles separately at (550 ℃, 650 ℃, 750 ℃, 850 ℃, and 950 ℃) for 2 hours each, with a ramping rate of 5℃/min. Finally these prepared samples were given for various characterizations as discussed below.

Synthesis_Procedure: The starting materials used in this study were BaCO3, Fe2O3, and Al2O3. A mixture of 1BaCO3+5Fe2O3+Al2O3 plus an excess of 10% of BaCO3 was loaded into a hardened steel vial together with fifteen 10 mm steel balls. The excess of BaCO3 can benefit the formation of single Ba-ferrite phase [9–12]. 20 g of the mixture were mechanically milled for 36 h using a Fritsch planetary ball mill (pulverisette 5) under air atmosphere. A ball-to-powder mass charge ratio of 10:1 was chosen. The as-milled powder was annealed for 1 h at temperatures between 700 and 1300°C. For comparison, BaCO3+6Fe2O3 plus 10% of excess of BaCO3 (i.e. without Al substitution) were mechanically milled under the same conditions as described above. The as-milled powder was annealed for 1 h at different temperatures from 700 to 1200°C.

Synthesis_Procedure: Stoichiometric amount of Fe(NO3)3 was dissolved in distilled water and quantitatively precipitated by concentrated ammonia in solution, then the precipitate was washed with water until neutrality removes the anion NO3. A little amount of SrSO4 with the atomic ratio Fe:Sr=11.6:1 was added, and a homogeneous transparent solution was achieved in a few seconds. This solution, to which stoichiometric amount of ethylene glycol was added, was slowly evaporated at 60°C until a high viscous residual was formed and a gel was developed during heating at 180°C. The gel was annealed at temperatures between 500°C and 1000°C for 5h at a rate of 4.5°C/min. Before annealing, the gel was preheated to 450°C using the same rates to decompose the organic precursor.

Synthesis_Procedure: Two different methods were employed to prepare pure (BaFe12O19) and ZnTi-doped $BaO 5.7@Fe22x(ZnTi)xO3#% spherical BaFe particles: semicoprecipitation ~SC! and ultrasonic spray pyrolysis ~UP! methods. In the SC method, well-separated nanosized spherical Fe3O4 ~0.2–0.3 μm! precursors were synthesized by aging Fe~OH!2 at 95°C in deaerated solution with a pH ~6 to 7!, followed by mixing with colloidal BaCO3 and additives, Zn~OH!2 and Ti~OH!4, at pH.11. A molar ratio of equivalent doped cations, x5~Zn and Ti!/Fe, was 0.18. The dried mixture was calcined at various temperatures in the range of 600–1000°C for 2 h in air and followed by a wet milling process to improve dispersibility and remove the NaCl byproduct. The synthetic solution was then vaporized using an ultrasonic nebulizer at the operating frequency of 1.7 MHz. Generated mist was introduced into the quartz tube inside a furnace, which was at 900°C, while evacuating the tube with a vacuum pump. Residence time of mist in the quartz tube was estimated to be about 1.5 s. Spherical amorphous precursors were collected from two different sites: one sample from a collector tube at 150°C and the other from a watertrap bottle. These collected particles were subjected to calcination at a temperature above 600°C for 2 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Two different methods were employed to prepare pure (BaFe12O19) and ZnTi-doped $BaO 5.7@Fe22x(ZnTi)xO3#% spherical BaFe particles: semicoprecipitation ~SC! and ultrasonic spray pyrolysis ~UP! methods. In the SC method, well-separated nanosized spherical Fe3O4 ~0.2–0.3 μm! precursors were synthesized by aging Fe~OH!2 at 95°C in deaerated solution with a pH ~6 to 7!, followed by mixing with colloidal BaCO3 and additives, Zn~OH!2 and Ti~OH!4, at pH.11. A molar ratio of equivalent doped cations, x5~Zn and Ti!/Fe, was 0.18. The dried mixture was calcined at various temperatures in the range of 600–1000°C for 2 h in air and followed by a wet milling process to improve dispersibility and remove the NaCl byproduct. In the UP method, the starting materials were Ba~NO3!2 and Fe~NO3)3•9H2O with additives ZnCl2 and TiCl4. Total metallic ion concentration of a synthetic solution was adjusted to 0.05 M where the value x of BaO 5.7@Fe22x(ZnTi!xO3# was the same as the above molar ratio. The synthetic solution was then vaporized using an ultrasonic nebulizer at the operating frequency of 1.7 MHz. Generated mist was introduced into the quartz tube inside a furnace, which was at 900°C, while evacuating the tube with a vacuum pump. Residence time of mist in the quartz tube was estimated to be about 1.5 s. Spherical amorphous precursors were collected from two different sites: one sample from a collector tube at 150°C and the other from a watertrap bottle. These collected particles were subjected to calcination at a temperature above 600°C for 2 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: The fuels ODH, MDH and MH have been prepared as reported earlier. The composition of the redox mixture for combustion has been calculated from the oxidising valencies of the metal nitrates and the reducing valency of the fuel based on the propellant chemistry and keeping the equivalence ratio unity (O/F=1). BaFe12O19 was obtained by rapidly heating an aqueous concentrated solution of barium nitrate (0.54 gm), ferric nitrate (10 gm) and ODH (4.60 gm)/MDH (3.24 gm)/MH (2.74 gm) at 350°C in a preheated muffle furnace. The solution in a 300 cm3 pyrex dish initially boils, undergoes rapid dehydration and foaming followed by the appearance of large number of sparks to yield voluminous oxide. In the case of MDH process flame was seen at the end of combustion (flame temp ~900°C).

Synthesis_Procedure: As raw material for the production of fine-crystalline BHF, iron oxides (γ-Fe2O3) or iron oxihydroxide (FeOOH) and oxide or hydroxide or nitrate or nitrite of barium were used. The preassigned amounts of precursors were mixed up dry or as water suspension. Beforehand each of the precursors was grinded in ball mill or in the mortar and was sifted through the sieve (0.25 mm). Then the reactants were intermixed and were sifted 2-3 times. The obtained mixture was loaded into the container of the autoclave, and then the container was located in the autoclave, For the creation of necessary water vapor pressure, the bottom of the autoclave outside of the container was filled up with water. For merging water suspension of reactants two procedures were used: (1) reactants mixed in water were dried at the temperature of 50–70°C, then the dry mixture was grinded in mortar and sifted; (2) humid mixture of suspensions of reactants was loaded into the container of autoclave. The autoclave was sealed hermetically and located in the furnace, which has before been heated up to temperature in the interval 200-400°C. The synthesis was proceeded in laboratory autoclaves with a volume of 16cm3, and also in half-industrial autoclaves (volume 501). With the aim of optimization of the process the following parameters were varied: content of the initial mixture and ratio of reactants in respect of Fe203/Ba0, temperature TVT in the range 200–400°C, pressure of water vapor in the range 10-30 MPa and time of synthesis.

Synthesis_Procedure: M-type barium ferrites co-substituted with Co and Ti for Fe, Ba(CoTi)xFe12–2xO19 were synthesized using analytical grade BaCO3, Fe2O3, Co2O3 and TiO2 via solid state reactions. The x value was varied as x = 0.00, 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80, 1.00, 1.15, 1.20, 1.25 and 1.30. The raw materials are in powder form. The powders were mixed using a ball mill for 16 h in a teflon vial with zirconia balls and deionized water as the milling media. The mixed powder was dried and then pre-sintered at 1100 °C for 4 h in air. The pre-sintered powder was milled again for 12 h in deionized water. After drying, the powder was granulated by adding 8 wt% of polyvinyl alcohol as a binder and pressed into 2–3 mm thick plates or rings. The compacted samples were sintered at 1175 °C for 6 h.

Synthesis_Procedure: Pure iron chloride—FeCl3.6H2O (Merck) and pure barium chloride—BaCl2.2H2O (Merck) were used as raw materials. The Fe/Ba molar ratios (n) used were 10, 10.5, and 11. Three different pH values were investigated (11, 12 and 12.5). In preparation, the aqueous solution of NaOH/Na2CO3 (5:1) was poured drop by drop onto an aqueous solution of ferric chloride and barium chloride. Vigorous stirring was used until the desired pH was attained. The coprecipitated thus obtained was dried and powdered in an agate mortar. The dried powders were calcinated in a tubular furnace under an oxygen atmosphere at 860°C, 920°C and 1000°C for 1.5 h. After calcination the obtained powders were repeatedly washed with hot water to eliminate the excess of NaCl formed during coprecipitation reaction. The residual water was removed by acetone.

Synthesis_Procedure: Samples were prepared, using a sol–gel technique,11,12 from five precursor solutions that had different compositions (see Table I). For precursor solutions A, C, and E, a stoichiometric amount of Fe(NO3)3z9H2O and Ba(NO3)2 was dissolved a citric acid aqueous solution and/or an ethylene glycol solution at 60°C, according to an Fe:Ba atomic ratio of 11:6. For precursor solutions B and D, a stoichiometric amount of Fe(NO3)3z9H2O was dissolved in distilled water and quantitatively precipitated with a concentrated ammonia solution. The precipitate, which was washed with water until neutrality was attained, to remove the NO3 − anion, was then dissolved in a citric acid solution (precursor solution B) or a mixed solution of citric acid and ethylene glycol (precursor solution D) at a temperature of 60°C. A stoichiometric amount of BaCO3 was added, and a completely homogeneous transparent solution was achieved within a few seconds. These solutions were slowly evaporated until a highly viscous residue was formed, and a gel was developed during heating in a temperature range of 140°–180°C. Corresponding samples were obtained by treating the gel with a different heating process.

For precursor solutions A, C, and E, a stoichiometric amount of Fe(NO3)3z9H2O and Ba(NO3)2 was dissolved a citric acid aqueous solution and/or an ethylene glycol solution at 60°C, according to an Fe:Ba atomic ratio of 11:6. For precursor solutions B and D, a stoichiometric amount of Fe(NO3)3z9H2O was dissolved in distilled water and quantitatively precipitated with a concentrated ammonia solution. The precipitate, which was washed with water until neutrality was attained, to remove the NO3 − anion, was then dissolved in a citric acid solution (precursor solution B) or a mixed solution of citric acid and ethylene glycol (precursor solution D) at a temperature of 60°C. A stoichiometric amount of BaCO3 was added, and a completely homogeneous transparent solution was achieved within a few seconds. These solutions were slowly evaporated until a highly viscous residue was formed, and a gel was developed during heating in a temperature range of 140°–180°C. Corresponding samples were obtained by treating the gel with a different heating process.

Synthesis_Procedure: 2.1 出発 原 料 本 実 験 に は, 有 機 金 属 化 合 物 の バ リ ウ ム エ トキ シ ド Ba(OC2H5)2(Ba(OEt)2と 略 す), トリス アセ チ ル アセ ト ナ ー ト鉄 (Ⅲ) Fe(CH3COCHCOCH3)3 (同Fe(acac)3) お よ び ビ ス ア セ チ ル ア セ トナ ー トジ ア ク ア コバ ル ト(Ⅱ) Co(CH3COCHCOCH3)2(H2O)2 (同CO(acac)2(H2O)2) を用 い た. Ba(OEt)2は 金 属 バ リ ウム (半 井 化 学 薬 品 製 特 級) と脱 水 精 製 した無 水 エ タ ノー ル の 反 応 に よ り合 成 し, エ タ ノー ル 溶 液 と し て 用 い た. Fe(acac)3とCO (acac)2 (H2O)2は 安 定 な キ レー ト化 合 物 で あ り, 市 販 の 高 純 度 試 薬 (同 仁 化 学 研 究 所 製, 純 度99.9%) を用 い た. 2.2 合 成 法 Ba(OEt)2, Fe(acac)3お よ びCO(acac)2(H2O)2を モ ル比 でBa:Fe:Co=1:12‑x:xの バ リ ウ ム ヘ キ サ フ ェ ラ イ トの 化 学 量 論 組 成 に な る よ うに 調合 し, 濃 度 がBa(OEt)2は2.0×10‑3mol/l, Fe(acac)3とCO(acac)2 (H2O), は2.4×10‑2mol/lの 無 水 エ タ ノ ー ル 溶 液 を用 い た. こ の原 料 溶 液 を油 浴 で約60℃ に 昇 温 後, 脱 イ オ ン水 で5倍 に 希 釈 し た ア ン モ ニ ア 水 を 滴 下 し, pHを 11.0か ら11.5に 調 節 しな が ら加 水 分 解 し た後, 3時 間 還 流 した. この 懸 濁 液 を分 画分 子 量30000の 限外 瀘 過 膜 を用 い て 窒 素 圧 力5kg/cm2の 加 圧 下 で 限外 瀘 過 し, さ ら にpHを 調 節 した ア ンモ ニ ア水 で洗 浄 した. 分 離 した 沈 殿 は 電 子 レ ン ジ で 乾 燥 後, 空 気 中 に お い て 約 3℃/minで 昇 温 後, 所 定 温 度 で1時 間 加 熱 処 理 し炉 内 にて 放 冷 した.

Fe(acac)3とCO (acac)2 (H2O)2は 安 定 な キ レー ト化 合 物 で あ り, 市 販 の 高 純 度 試 薬 (同 仁 化 学 研 究 所 製, 純 度99.9%) を用 い た. 2.2 合 成 法 Ba(OEt)2, Fe(acac)3お よ びCO(acac)2(H2O)2を モ ル比 でBa:Fe:Co=1:12‑x:xの バ リ ウ ム ヘ キ サ フ ェ ラ イ トの 化 学 量 論 組 成 に な る よ うに 調合 し, 濃 度 がBa(OEt)2は2.0×10‑3mol/l, Fe(acac)3とCO(acac)2 (H2O), は2.4×10‑2mol/lの 無 水 エ タ ノ ー ル 溶 液 を用 い た. こ の原 料 溶 液 を油 浴 で約60℃ に 昇 温 後, 脱 イ オ ン水 で5倍 に 希 釈 し た ア ン モ ニ ア 水 を 滴 下 し, pHを 11.0か ら11.5に 調 節 しな が ら加 水 分 解 し た後, 3時 間 還 流 した. この 懸 濁 液 を分 画分 子 量30000の 限外 瀘 過 膜 を用 い て 窒 素 圧 力5kg/cm2の 加 圧 下 で 限外 瀘 過 し, さ ら にpHを 調 節 した ア ンモ ニ ア水 で洗 浄 した. 分 離 した 沈 殿 は 電 子 レ ン ジ で 乾 燥 後, 空 気 中 に お い て 約 3℃/minで 昇 温 後, 所 定 温 度 で1時 間 加 熱 処 理 し炉 内 にて 放 冷 した.

Fe(acac)3とCO (acac)2 (H2O)2は 安 定 な キ レー ト化 合 物 で あ り, 市 販 の 高 純 度 試 薬 (同 仁 化 学 研 究 所 製, 純 度99.9%) を用 い た. 2.2 合 成 法 Ba(OEt)2, Fe(acac)3お よ びCO(acac)2(H2O)2を モ ル比 でBa:Fe:Co=1:12‑x:xの バ リ ウ ム ヘ キ サ フ ェ ラ イ トの 化 学 量 論 組 成 に な る よ うに 調合 し, 濃 度 がBa(OEt)2は2.0×10‑3mol/l, Fe(acac)3とCO(acac)2 (H2O), は2.4×10‑2mol/lの 無 水 エ タ ノ ー ル 溶 液 を用 い た. こ の原 料 溶 液 を油 浴 で約60℃ に 昇 温 後, 脱 イ オ ン水 で5倍 に 希 釈 し た ア ン モ ニ ア 水 を 滴 下 し, pHを 11.0か ら11.5に 調 節 しな が ら加 水 分 解 し た後, 3時 間 還 流 した. この 懸 濁 液 を分 画分 子 量30000の 限外 瀘 過 膜 を用 い て 窒 素 圧 力5kg/cm2の 加 圧 下 で 限外 瀘 過 し, さ ら にpHを 調 節 した ア ンモ ニ ア水 で洗 浄 した. 分 離 した 沈 殿 は 電 子 レ ン ジ で 乾 燥 後, 空 気 中 に お い て 約 3℃/minで 昇 温 後, 所 定 温 度 で1時 間 加 熱 処 理 し炉 内 にて 放 冷 した.

Fe(acac)3とCO (acac)2 (H2O)2は 安 定 な キ レー ト化 合 物 で あ り, 市 販 の 高 純 度 試 薬 (同 仁 化 学 研 究 所 製, 純 度99.9%) を用 い た. 2.2 合 成 法 Ba(OEt)2, Fe(acac)3お よ びCO(acac)2(H2O)2を モ ル比 でBa:Fe:Co=1:12‑x:xの バ リ ウ ム ヘ キ サ フ ェ ラ イ トの 化 学 量 論 組 成 に な る よ うに 調合 し, 濃 度 がBa(OEt)2は2.0×10‑3mol/l, Fe(acac)3とCO(acac)2 (H2O), は2.4×10‑2mol/lの 無 水 エ タ ノ ー ル 溶 液 を用 い た. こ の原 料 溶 液 を油 浴 で約60℃ に 昇 温 後, 脱 イ オ ン水 で5倍 に 希 釈 し た ア ン モ ニ ア 水 を 滴 下 し, pHを 11.0か ら11.5に 調 節 しな が ら加 水 分 解 し た後, 3時 間 還 流 した. この 懸 濁 液 を分 画分 子 量30000の 限外 瀘 過 膜 を用 い て 窒 素 圧 力5kg/cm2の 加 圧 下 で 限外 瀘 過 し, さ ら にpHを 調 節 した ア ンモ ニ ア水 で洗 浄 した. 分 離 した 沈 殿 は 電 子 レ ン ジ で 乾 燥 後, 空 気 中 に お い て 約 3℃/minで 昇 温 後, 所 定 温 度 で1時 間 加 熱 処 理 し炉 内 にて 放 冷 した.

Synthesis_Procedure: BaM-type hexaferrite powders with the general formula BaFe12O19 (BFO), Ba0.95Ca0.05Fe12O19 (BCFO), and Ba0.95Ca0.05Fe12−xCoxO19 (0 < x ≤ 0.4) (BCFCO) were synthesized by the conventional solid-phase method. The raw materials were selected from BaCO3 (99%, Aladdin Scientific Corp., Shanghai, China), Co3O4 (99%, Aladdin Scientific Corp., Shanghai, China), and Fe2O3 (99%, Aladdin Scientific Corp., Shanghai, China), and CaCO3 (>99%, AladdinScientificCorp., Shanghai, China)producedbyAladdinLtd. For the synthesis of the materials, different stoichiometric ratios of chemicals were used, depending on the target composition. Specifically, BaFe12O19 was prepared using 1 mole of BaCO3 and 6 moles of Fe2O3. Ba0.95Ca0.05Fe12O19 was synthesized by combining 0.95 moles of BaCO3, 0.05 moles of CaCO3, and 6 moles of Fe2O3. For Ba0.95Ca0.05CoxFe12−xO19 (where x represents the moles of Co), the preparation involved 0.95 moles of BaCO3, 0.05 moles of CaCO3, x/3 moles of Co3O4, and (12 − x)/2 moles of Fe2O3. After mixing the ingredients in stoichiometric ratios, deionized water, zirconia ball-mill beads, and the mixed ingredients were mixed in a ball milling jar in a ratio of 1:1:4 and placed in a planetary ball mill, in which the ball milling rate is 400 rpm for 4 h. The mixture was dried at 110 ◦C for 12 h and reground. The powder was then placed in a muffle furnace and calcined at 1000 ◦C for 2 h with a temperature-increase rate of 5 ◦C/min. The pre-calcined powder was then pelletized and milled for half an hour, with the addition of 5% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA). Toroidal specimens (outside diameter of 7 mm, inside diameter of 3 mm, and thickness of 3~5 mm) were pressed at 20 MPa. Finally, these samples were placed in a muffle furnace and sintered at 1200 ◦C for 2 h, with a ramp rate of 5 ◦C/min.

Synthesis_Procedure: Pb substituted Ba-Sr hexaferrites were prepared by the simple solid state reaction method.
